en: New Commentary on the *Ullambana Sūtra* (with Preface), composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Qiāntáng.
The Teaching is the gateway to the Way, and filial piety is the root of practice. Since [beings] have sunk into the darkness and forgotten their origins, compassion flows forth.
Out of compassionate entrustment to those kinsmen, this ultimate teaching was brought forth.
Now, the practitioner is that which seeks the Way; the sūtra is that which explains practice; the commentary (*śāstra*) is that which penetrates the sūtra;
and the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) is that which elucidates the commentary.
This is indeed the primary source for the initiation of name-and-teaching (mingjiao) and the essential method for lecturing on and discussing the learning.

In this degenerate age, worldly excesses have caused the True Teaching to fragment; lacking the transmission of a master, people follow their own reckless simplifications, competing for sharpness of rhetoric and displaying a profusion of memorized knowledge.
They employ private biases and wandering sophistry to launch cross-attacks against the conventional scriptures.

"How could one not contemplate cultivating the self to repay the virtues [of the Buddhas], yet instead merely pursue profit and live for fame? This is to辜负 (gu fù) the gift of life and betray Heaven and Earth.
This arises because those who transmit [the teachings] are rarely able to provide guidance and inspiration, while those who compose [treatises] each have their own flaws."
Therefore, I have taken up the brush to compile this new record, prioritizing brevity in expression and excellence in meaning.
Its teachings follow a systematic path and its principles converge upon what is most correct.
It is my hope that students may reach the commentaries through these records, penetrate the scriptures through the commentaries, and give rise to practice through the scriptures.
By practicing these deeds one constructs the Way;
thereafter, it spreads throughout the four seas and is bestowed upon future generations without ceasing day or night— is this not found within these writings?
[Commentary] *The Commentary on the Ullambana Sūtra* (including the Preface).
[Record] The explanation of the title of the sūtra is already fully contained within the text of the commentary; here, I shall briefly analyze it according to five sections:

first, distinguishing the subject and object; second, distinguishing the general and the specific; third, clarifying the Chinese and Sanskrit terms; fourth, explaining the establishment of the title; fifth, demonstrating similarities and differences. Regarding the first:

Based on the title of the original sutra, adding the seven characters "Spoken by the Buddha" (*buddhabhāṣita*), the commentary treats these as the "explicator" (*nirukta*) for the six characters above, while the sutra itself is treated as the "explicated" (*nirucya*).
Furthermore, the "basin" (*pén*) is the "savior" (*trātṛ*) and "Ullambana" is the "saved" (*trātavya*);

the "Buddha" is the "speaker" (*vaktṛ*) and the subsequent portion is the "spoken" (*vākya*). Regarding the two types of titles—the general and the specific—this shall first be discussed according to the title of the sutra.

The Buddha stated that the four characters "is this" (*shi tong*) apply generally to the following [text], while "of the distinction" (*wei bie*) applies specifically; furthermore, the character "sutra" (*jing zi*) applies generally to the preceding three characters, while "of the distinction" (*wei bie*) applies specifically;

and finally, the character "commentary" (*shu zi*) applies generally to the entire title of the sutra, while "of the distinction" (*wei bie*) applies specifically. By taking these specific terms to distinguish them from the general ones, the present sutra and the present commentary are thus delimited.

Third, regarding the Chinese and Sanskrit terms: "Buddha" (*fo*) and "Ullambana" (*yu lan quan*) are entirely Sanskrit terms; they are translated according to their meaning as "giving rise to goodness."
Furthermore, regarding the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Repaying Kindness), which was translated from Sanskrit into Chinese, every single character is entirely in the Chinese language.

As for the four types of titles established at the beginning of a sutra, they do not exceed three categories: person (*pudgala*), dharma, and metaphor (*upamā*). These may appear individually or in combination, resulting in seven distinct variations.
This sutra takes its title by fully incorporating all three: "Buddha" refers to the person; "Alaṃbana" (the bowl) serves as the metaphor.
The sub-commentary (*śū*) states: "The soul sinks into the dark path, and its life is like being hung upside down. Thus, the character *pen* (盆) is the *dharmaparyāya*. The *Fajing jing* says:
"I shall now explain the method for rescue and relief," which refers to the *pen-gong* (盆供). Based on the sub-commentary, this is the interpretation;

however, according to the phonetic glosses of the sutra, *pen* is also a Sanskrit term translated as "hanging upside down," and thus the person [in the painting] is used as a metaphor for the title. Five: Similarities and Differences.
According to Master Ying’s *Jīngyīnyì* (Explanations of the Pronunciation and Meaning of the Scriptures), the Sanskrit term is *ulambana*, which is translated here as "hanging upside down.

Examining this in detail, *ula* is simply *yulan* (盂蘭), and *bana* is the modern *pen* (盆). Thus, all three characters are originally Sanskrit terms that have merely undergone phonetic corruption and transformation.
The commentator of the sub-commentary (*shūzhǔ*) has, for the time being, based himself on the scriptural text and established the use of the character *pen*.
The words within [the commentary] are therefore rendered in elegant (hua) Chinese; as for the explanation of the phonology and meaning, the Sanskrit term is "de-shi" (attaining reality).

The commentators, however, generally concur with the sutra and harbor doubts, thus they have preserved both versions for people to choose from according to their own preferences. (Tradition holds that the Song Tripiṭaka Master said "U-kan-pa-na-pen-tso-na" translates as "an inverted hanging vessel for rescue," but as no authoritative source has been seen, I do not dare to accept it.
"Shu" (commentary/sparse) is explained as "sparse" (shu), meaning to resolve the meanings of the text so that there are no obstructions.
"Combined with the Preface" means that the title of the commentary is used concurrently with the heading of the preface; this is annotated here to show that the composition was intended for brevity.
[Commentary] Recorded by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Chongguo.
[Commentary]: Chongguo is a specific designation for a county and town; it currently belongs to Guozhou. The *Jiuzhou Dilili Ji* (Record of Geography of the Nine Provinces) states:
"Chongguo was the state of the Bazi during the Han dynasty. Later, because the local customs and character were flourishing (*chongsheng*), it was named accordingly.

During the reign of Emperor Ling of the Later Han, it was divided into two counties, Nan-chong and Xi-chong, by omitting the character 'guo' (state). According to the *Book of Jin*, regarding geography...

According to the *Lizhi*, there were both Xichongguo County and Nanchongguo County within Baxi Commandery; thus, we know that "Chongguo" was originally the full name [of the commandery], similar to cases such as Qiaoguó, Paiguó, and Luguó.
The author of the commentary was a native of Xichong County, so he follows the ancient name and simply refers to it as "Chongguo.
If one were to rely on other texts, they would generally specify the place of residence; however, in this case, [the author] has done so.
Since the essence of the sutras lies in the Way of Filial Piety, [Zongmi] designated it as the "Land of His Parents.

Furthermore, because he returned to his hometown to request the teachings, he recorded the place where he composed the work. Zongmi was the name of the commentator; born during the Tang Dynasty, he widely propagated the ultimate teachings.
While living in seclusion at Mount Guifeng in Zhongnan, people referred to him as "Guifeng. Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title of a Buddhist Patriarch.
The various traces of Master Dinghui’s transformation [of sentient beings] are all recorded in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty).
The interpretation by the śramaṇa Yu is as usual.

[Commentary: Beginning with the primordial chaos (*hundun*) and pervading heaven and earth, it unites humans and spirits and penetrates the noble and the humble; both Confucians and Buddhists take it as their fundamental principle.
This is none other than the Way of Filial Piety. [Commentary:

The first phrase praises its depth in the vertical dimension; the next four phrases praise its breadth in the horizontal dimension; the final phrase concludes by indicating that which is being praised.
"Vertical" refers to tracing back to the origin, wherein nothing precedes the primordial chaos (*hundun*); "horizontal" refers to manifesting its all-pervasive reach.

If one is partial, there is no emergence from the Three Powers (the Sage, the People, and the Spirits). To describe them as "vertically deep and horizontally vast" exhausts the praise for filial piety.

As for those who speak of the "primordial chaos" (*hundun*), the Confucian school maintains that Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are rooted in the Qi of the Primordial Chaos (*hun-yuan*). From this primal Qi, Heaven and Earth are produced;

from Heaven and Earth, the myriad things are produced. Thus, whether one is foolish or wise, noble or base, poor or wealthy, suffering or joyful—all these are traced back to the Mandate of Heaven, as are birth and death.
All transformations ultimately return to the One Qi (One Vital Energy). However, before Heaven and Earth and Yin and Yang were yet differentiated, the clear and the turbid were in mutual harmony;
therefore, it was named "Chun-hun" (the Undifferentiated Chaos). This is the ultimate doctrine of the Confucian school.

Next, the Daoists maintain that the Great Way of Non-being (Vimala) generates and nurtures all things; since the Way follows its own nature and arises from Original Qi, they say, "The Way gives birth to the One."
The Primordial Unity gives birth to Two (Heaven and Earth); Two gives birth to Three (the Three Powers); from the Three are born the myriad things.
The myriad things return to their root and revert to emptiness and stillness—this is the ultimate pinnacle of the Daoist teaching.

If we discuss the Buddhist teaching, according to the Hinayana perspective, it is said that all sentient beings, through the three poisons and the three karmas, construct the vessel-world, which undergoes the four phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness in cyclic succession.
Each cycle lasts twenty kalpas. Regarding the formation of the world at the beginning of the *khaṇḍa-kalpa* (empty kalpa), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"In the empty realm, a great wind arises; its lateral breadth is immeasurable. Even a diamond could not destroy it; this is called the 'Wind that Sustains the Realm' (*dhātu-dhāra-vāyu*).

(In Daoism, the Way takes the empty realm as the void; in Confucianism, the great wind is taken as the primordial chaos; this corresponds to what the Daoists call 'the Way gives birth to the One. Light-Sound [Devas], Golden-Treasury [Clouds] spread forth, reaching across the three thousand [worlds]."

The rain from the realms falls like chariot axles, but the downward wind obstructs it so that it cannot flow; first the realm of Brahmā is formed, extending down to the Yāma Heaven (the Confucians say those who are pure ascend to heaven).

The wind and waves stir the clear water to form Mount Sumeru and the seven golden mountains, while the dregs and turbidity become the earth and mountains, the four continents, the hells, the salt ocean, and the outer Cakravāḍa mountains (the Confucians say those who are turbid become the earthly way; this refers to "one producing two"). Only then is it called a "realm" (*dhātu*).
The receptacle world is established over the course of one *kalpa* of increase and decrease (meaning the world is only fully formed after one *kalpa* of increase and decrease has passed).

Eventually, when the merit of the second dhyāna is exhausted, beings descend to be born among humans. [In the Way, this is called] "two births" (*dō*), while in the Three Teachings, it is called "Pangu being born from within. Initially, they ate earth-cakes and forest creepers;

later, they consumed non-glutinous rice, which they could not digest, leading to the emergence of excrement and urine, as well as the differentiation of male and female forms. They then divided the fields, established lords, and sought ministers and assistants.

The various distinctions (the Way refers to the three [stages] that give birth to the myriad things; the Confucian school is likewise) total nineteen. Including the increases and decreases, they total twenty.

These increases and decreases are called the *siddha-kalpa* (the kalpa of formation). (The kalpas of abiding, destruction, and emptiness each last twenty kalpas. Guifeng said: "During the kalpa of the realm of emptiness, the Daoist teaching designates it as the Way of Non-being (*xuwu*).
The 'Great Wind' is precisely that which the Confucian school calls the single qi of chaos (*hundun*). Thus we know the mixture [of these teachings].
The term *chun* (chaotic unity) refers to the beginning of the kalpa; at this time, the Way of Filial Piety was already latent within it, which is why it is said to "begin with" it.

(Both of the above citations are from Guifeng’s *Yuanren lun*; Gushan remarked: "It is not the case that non-Buddhist teachings of this land recognize the empty kalpa as chaotic unity. Question: Why do you now, in explaining Buddhist scriptures, rely instead on the Confucian school to speak of "chaotic unity"?
Answer: Practicing filial piety to repay one's parents is precisely intended to guide worldly customs; moreover, it serves as a means to establish [the truth] when returning to one's home.
To ensure that both monastics and laypeople may hear this together, if one were to point directly to the beginning of the kalpa, the common folk would find it difficult to understand;

therefore, by designating it as "chaos" (hundun), the fourfold assembly can all comprehend it. Furthermore, in clarifying the similarities and differences between the two teachings below, there are many citations from Confucian texts, the intent of which is likewise the same.
Mount Gu said: "Since the fundamental purport of this sutra belongs to the vehicle of humans and devas, it is appropriate to bring it close to Confucian texts."
As for the claim that "chaos" (hundun) exists, I say this is not so. Buddhism has already clarified the principle of retribution for humans and devas;
as a single path of expedient means to guide those of dull faculties, how could it be brought into proximity with the Confucian scriptures?

Even the realm of humans and devas cannot be compared [to the ultimate truth], let alone this sutra, which is not merely for humans and devas (as will be extensively refuted later). Next, to clarify the horizontal breadth, we first take up the Three Powers (the three sages). First:

The three phrases beginning with "Heaven and Earth" discuss the distinctions among human beings. Alternatively, "Heaven and Earth" may refer to insentient things, while those that follow refer to sentient beings.
Regarding "filling Heaven and Earth," this refers to what the *Xiaojing* says: "Now, filial piety is the constant way of Heaven" (*chang* meaning "constant";

it refers to the three luminaries shining down, the four seasons revolving, and all things deriving their life—this has been so from antiquity to the present, and is thus the constant virtue of Heaven). It is also "the righteousness of Earth" (*yi* meaning "benefit").

That the myriad things produced from mountains, marshes, forests, and fields flourish according to the suitability of their winds and soil is the benefit provided by the Earth. That the constant virtue of Heaven descends upon the realm is the filiality of Heaven;
that the Earth provides nourishment and sustenance for all living beings is the filiality of the Earth. Thus, it is clear that the Way of Filiality pervades the space between Heaven and Earth.
As for those who penetrate both the human and the divine, humans can be known; as for the divine, it is said: [text fragment]... that which is called the Divine.

Gods and ghosts collectively comprise the four realms of existence; though the heavens, humans, ghosts, and hells are distinguished by their hidden or manifest states, all possess sovereigns and parents.
Thus it is verified that the spirits of the unseen realm all know filial piety and reverence.

If one follows what is said below—that even the compassionate crow and the parrot understand how to repay kindness—then the Way of Filial Piety pervades the six realms of existence. (Some say, "One who practices filial piety moves the gods and ghosts," but this is not so. Furthermore, it penetrates both the noble and the humble.

In terms of human beings, the Son of Heaven is most noble, while the commoner is merely base; among the feudal lords and high ministers, those who look down are noble, while those who look up are base.

The *Classic of Filial Piety* has five chapters, each clarifying a specific application of filial conduct; though these five applications differ, the essence of filial conduct does not vary. Therefore, the concluding summary states:
"From the Son of Heaven down to the commoner, there is no difference in filial piety; it is only that some fail to carry it through from beginning to end, and thus suffer the affliction of its lack."

"Regarding the phrase 'and there has never been such a thing' (since death ends it, there is no beginning or end; one has never suffered from a lack of strength or failed to exercise restraint): that which both Confucians and Buddhists take as their fundamental principle is precisely what is demonstrated below regarding the Way of Filial Piety.
Herein, filial piety is clearly elucidated as the root and foundation of these two teachings. The commentary explains this in detail, so I shall not labor further with redundant words.
When lecturers encounter this text, they should explore and cite this teaching, for the convergence of the realms of humans and spirits transcends the distinctions of noble and base."
According to the positions held by both Confucians and Buddhists regarding the three types of karmic bonds (*saṃyojana*), only filial piety is uniquely designated as "exclusive" (*du*).

This means that while other practices are restricted to a single end, filial piety alone encompasses both [this world and the beyond]. By reviewing the various meanings cited above, this can be understood.
The *Erya* states: "To be good toward one's parents is called filial piety. Since every son ought to practice this, it is termed the "Way of Filial Piety" (*xiaodao*).

[Commentary] To respond to the earnest sincerity of a filial son and rescue his parents from suffering and distress—to repay the profound grace and virtue of Heaven—there is none other than the teaching of the *Ullambana* Bowl.

[Sub-commentary] "To respond" (*ying*) means to accord with or to honor. A "filial son" refers generally to those in the final age who seek to repay their parents; "earnest sincerity" (*ken-ch'eng*) refers to...
Its exclusive focus is on those who suffer through calamities and gaze upon the evil realms; its benevolent virtue does not extend beyond nurturing them with milk. The text consists of four phrases:
the first phrase identifies the recipients of the response (the capacity), and the last phrase concludes by indicating the teaching that responds to them.

The middle two phrases pertain generally to both the capacity and the teaching: in relation to the capacity, they refer to the matters to which one should respond; in relation to the teaching, they constitute the means by which one responds.
When applied, its efficacy accords with the principles of the subsequent scriptures, which possess four essential meanings: first, filial piety; second, making offerings; third, relieving suffering;

and fourth, repaying kindness. When compared with the present text, it lacks only the meaning of making offerings; this must necessarily be included to show that other scriptures do not fully contain all these meanings, and thus the word "only" is used.

[Commentary: Zongmi’s transgressions were such that he lost his parents in early childhood; he constantly experienced the sorrow of walking through snow and frost and harbored forever the resentment of the wind-blown tree.
[Record: The first two phrases describe the loss of his parents in youth; the next phrase indicates his lifelong mourning for them.

The phrase "regretting being unable to attend to his parents' needs" (*jùhèn bùjí shìyǎng*)—the character *xùn* here signifies "guilt. The meaning is that having failed in the service and nourishment of one's parents, one subsequently causes their death;
thus, taking the blame upon oneself, such a person is a transgressor. Regarding the phrase "grieving at the snow and frost during early years," when one was still a child:
the *Liji*, in the "Jiyi" (Meaning of Sacrifices), states, "When the autumn frost and dew have fallen, the superior man treads upon them and is inevitably moved to sorrow."

The sorrowful heart is not merely a matter of cold; when spring rain and dew have moistened all, a gentleman treading upon them must surely feel a sense of *chùtì* (the first character being *chǒu*, the second *lì*;

it signifies anxiety)—a feeling as if he were about to see [his ancestors] again. Now, to briefly cite an example from autumn, if one simply replaces the word "dew" (*lù*) with "frost" (*shù*), it applies equally to both autumn and winter.
As for the "resentment of wind-blown trees," the Annals of Lu state that when Confucius went out...
Xingjian saw Yu Quzi weeping by the roadside. (Yu Quzi was the Chancellor of the State of Chu. He asked him the reason for his grief, and he replied: "I have three failures, and for this I weep.
In my youth I traveled abroad to study, wandering throughout the world; yet my parents had already passed away, and I failed to attend to their needs—this is my first failure.
I have always held my aspirations high and refused to serve a mediocre ruler, yet I have not fulfilled my duties as a minister—this is my [second failure]."
"Secondly, I have lost my discernment; thirdly, my social circle is small and I lack close friends, so that in old age I have no one to rely upon—these are my three losses.
Indeed, when a tree wishes for stillness, the wind does not cease; when a son wishes to provide for his parents, they do not wait.
That which passes and does not return is youth; that which cannot be seen again is one's parents. Having spoken these words, he stood up, wept, and died. Kongzi [recorded this].
The Master looked back and said to those around him, "Take note of this; it may serve as a warning. Thereupon, twelve of his disciples took their leave to return home and care for their parents.
(The old citation from the *Jiayu* differs somewhat from this; I have followed the historical text for accuracy.
Now, I shall employ only one sentence from the text to illustrate how when one's actions and heart are at odds, one harbors long-lasting sighs and regrets.

[Commentary] I venture to say that although one may express filial thoughts through lifelong burial mounds and seasonal offerings throughout one's entire life, these do not assist the Way of the Spirits.
[Sub-commentary] The first two characters mark the mind capable of reflection; "I venture to say" (*qiè yǐ*) indicates private deliberation.

The following four phrases demonstrate the matters reflected upon. The first two phrases clarify the practice of Confucian conduct regarding the terms "lifelong" (*zhōngshēn*) and "throughout one's life" (*zúshì*), showing how the meanings shift.
Following the ancients, when parents had passed away, one would carry earth on one's back to form a mound and plant cypress trees in rows;

for three years, one would dwell in a hut by the tomb to exhaust one’s filial sincerity. Regarding "fén-lǒng" (mounds and graves): "fén" refers to a mound formed by piling up earth, while "mù" (grave) refers to the leveled ground;

"lǒng" is the precinct of the grave. "Zhēng-cháng" (steam-offering and seasonal sacrifice) are names for sacrifices; according to the *Liji*, there are four seasonal sacrifices: the spring sacrifice is called "yè" (pronounced yào), and the summer...
It is said that the *di* sacrifice is held in autumn and the *chang* sacrifice in winter; the text here briefly cites autumn and winter to illustrate the sacrificial rites.

However, regarding the practice of dwelling in a hut at the tomb for three years and performing sacrifices during the four seasons, according to the principles of ritual (li), these do not necessarily last a lifetime.

The present passage cites long-term practices to illustrate even more recent ones, thereby demonstrating their lack of merit. Although the latter two lines manifest their uselessness, the first line is concessive.
That is to say, the former two matters can only be applied to one's own mind; the latter phrase is a denial, meaning it is insufficient to assist those on the path to the underworld.
[Commentary] Thus, having searched through the teachings of the sages and worthies and reverently sought the methods for posthumous offerings, I have obtained this Dharma-gate in truth.
For many years, Miaoxing made offerings of the four requisites to the Triple Gem on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

[Commentary] The first two phrases describe his seeking of the Dharma through the study of the sūtras; the teachings of the sages and worthies do not exceed the Tripiṭaka. Regarding the Vinaya, it was spoken solely by the Buddha.
As for the Sūtras and Śāstras, they were spoken by the Buddha, as well as by his disciples, various ṛṣis, devas, and transformed persons. The Buddha is the ultimate sage, while his disciples—

The "Sons" (disciples) encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles and the Sages and Worthies: on the small scale, there are the Seven Worthies and Four Sages; on the great scale, there are the Three Worthies and Ten Sages.

Furthermore, the inclusion of Celestial Immortals (*tianxian*) indicates that the meaning extends to ordinary beings as well. "Seeking" (*suo*) is also explained as "to seek," referring to the methods of reverent practice.

The following four lines clarify that having attained these methods accords with one's aspirations; the first two lines praise the profundity of their merit, while the final two lines briefly demonstrate the practice.

In the first sutra of this section, it is recorded that when the Venerable Maudgalyāyana’s compassionate mother fell into the realm of hungry ghosts, her delusions and karma had become so deep that even his supernormal powers could not save her.

He was thus compelled to rely on a single day’s offering of a basin of water; by performing this brief act of veneration, he was able to cause her to be liberated from suffering in the netherworld at that very moment.
Since such a miraculous efficacy has been manifested, it may truly be called a divine method beyond the reach of thought or speech; therefore, it is termed a "wondrous practice. Next:
The "manifestation of conduct" (*caryā-prakāśana*) summarizes the four matters concerning worldly affairs found later in the sutra— namely, dwellings, clothing, food and drink,
and medicinal requisites— while the "Three Honored Ones" refers to the Triple Gem, both of which are revered by the world.
[Commentary] Zongmi has relied upon this [text] to practice and revere it for many years, while simultaneously lecturing on its teachings to demonstrate them to those who have not yet heard them.

[Sub-commentary] The first two phrases clarify the establishment of offerings; the latter two phrases indicate that practicing and revering the scripture oneself constitutes the practice of self-benefit (*svārtha*), while lecturing to demonstrate it to others constitutes the practice of benefiting others (*parārtha*).
"Teachings" (*gào*) refers to the Buddha’s injunctions, specifically pointing to this very sutra.

[Commentary] Now, upon returning to his hometown, he established a dharma assembly according to the [imperial] decree; the elders among both the clergy and the laity were moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy, and with one voice they requested him to compose a new commentary.

[Record] The first two phrases clarify his return to his hometown and the inauguration of the assembly, which occurred when he was summoned during the second year of the Dàhé era (828 CE) of Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty.
In the inner palace, he consulted on the essentials of the Dharma and subsequently requested leave to return to the mountains (intending to go to Zhongnan).

Later, at the request of the assembly, he entered Shu to establish stele inscriptions for the ancestral masters of former generations. From there, he returned to his hometown; as it happened to be the end of the summer retreat, he said, "relying on the days," etc.
"Kai" means to open a lecture series, and "she" means to provide offerings. The second couplet indicates the two groups of followers: the monastics and the laity.

The statement "comprehensively encompassing the four divisions" refers to the *Qilü* (Rites of Five Decades), which states: at age fifty, one is called *ài* (the hair turns white like mugwort); at age sixty, one is called *qí* (*qí* also means old). Regarding the expression of sorrow and joy:
one feels sorrow upon hearing of the profound kindness of one's parents and harboring a sense of poignant gratitude;

one feels joy because one has obtained the opportunity for retribution and is now able to follow and practice the supreme Dharma. The final two lines clarify the circumstances for composing this commentary.

"Different mouths" refers to the fact that those who make the request are not uniform; "not a single sound" refers to the fact that that which is requested is without variation. This is stated in contrast to what was previously described, hence it is called the "New Commentary.

This is precisely what is meant by the citation of the Tripiṭaka Master below, beginning with the words "as it says... Question: Since there were already commentaries from antiquity, why must this one be newly produced?
Answer: Those ancient texts have already been lost, so their relative merits cannot be known. Nevertheless, in establishing the present and abolishing the past, it is certainly not for nothing.
However, fearing that the fundamental tenets might differ, or that the interpretations might be erroneous, or that the work might be overly ornate and lack substance,
or too plain and lacking in literary refinement— so as to ensure it harmonizes with the various capacities of beings and circulates through a hundred generations—
I have composed this text in response to the requests of many.

[Commentary] "The mind dwells among the pines and cypresses; how could one neglect the local community? To truly accord with the sentiments of those who have come, I shall expound upon the essential Way.
[Record] The first two lines express his own feelings; the latter two lines grant permission for the request.

"Pines and cypresses" refers to the trees planted at gravesites, using these objects to represent one's parents. "Local community" (*xiānglǚ*)—*lǚ* being the gates of a village—refers to the neighborhood.

To "dwell" (chu) means to treat them as elders; "to honor" (shi-jing) means to be truly compliant. "To initiate" (fa) refers to acting as the originator, and "to spread" (hui) refers to causing it to circulate.

Although the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same: this specifically refers to the dharma-gate of making offerings to repay one's parents, which is established in this sutra, as being the ultimate essential.

[Commentary: I bow my head to the Lord of the Three Realms, the Greatly Filial Śākyamuni Honored One, who through kalpas of recompensing parental kindness and accumulating causes has attained Perfect Enlightenment.
[Record: When the masters of both the Western Land and this region compose their works, they invariably first establish verses to pay homage to the Triple Gem. This is because...
The term "one who seeks" (*su*) has six meanings: first, because of bearing [the Buddha's] grace; second, because of seeking protection; third, because of causing faith to arise;

fourth, because of manifesting respectful decorum; fifth, because of revealing excellence; and sixth, because of opening sentient beings to mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha (as cited in the *Nanshan Jieben Shu*).
Nevertheless, although the Three Jewels have various manifestations of transformation, modes of abiding, and ontological essences, their fundamental substance is one and all-pervasive.
The dimensions [of the prostration] are as clarified elsewhere; for now, I shall explain this verse based on its manifested form (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*).

In the first verse, the first two characters refer to the ritual of veneration (*pūjā-vidhi*): when about to compose the commentary, one first pays homage. The physical form manifests mental reverence, as the head and crown touch the ground;

thus it is called "bowing the head" (*kai-shou*), where *kai* means to bend down and *shou* means to reach. The phrase "the three realms and below" refers to the objects of veneration (*pūjya-viṣaya*).

The first two phrases cite the name; the latter two phrases praise his virtues. The three realms are the sphere of those to be converted—the desire, form, and formless realms encompassing the great trichiliocosm—wherein the Buddha acts as the converting master. This is as the Sūtra says: "Now these three realms are all mine;
the sentient beings therein are all my sons. Great filial piety is the causal practice of Śākyamuni.
Although the virtues of the Honored One’s fruition and practice are ten thousandfold, filial piety (*xiao*) is raised as the principle that encompasses them all;

although his virtues are immeasurable, they are collectively subsumed under the name "Śākya. While the term "Śākya" specifically refers to the Teacher, "Great Filial Piety" applies universally to all Buddhas.

"Śākyamuni" is translated as "Able Benevolent One" (*Nengren*) and "Silent Stillness" (*Jimo*); because of this silent stillness, he does not abide in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), which is the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, because he is the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni), he does not abide in nirvana; this is precisely what is meant by "retribution and response.

Within the praise of his virtues, the first phrase explains the aforementioned "supreme filial piety," while the second phrase explains the aforementioned "Venerable Śākya. Regarding his repayment of kindness over successive kalpas, we must distinguish between the general and the specific.
Generally speaking, the six perfections and myriad practices are all acts of repaying kindness. Specifically, it refers to serving one's parents in every place.

All were able to fulfill filial piety to the point of attaining the Way; first they delivered their compassionate parents, beginning with preaching the Dharma to Māyā as she ascended to heaven, and finally, for Śuddhodana, they personally carried his coffin.
Having accomplished their merit over kalpas, they are thus called "Greatly Filial. Those who accumulated causes stepped toward the supreme [state] to repay their parents;
having realized perfect enlightenment, they manifested the fulfillment of the present fruit. In Sanskrit, this is called *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. The term "perfect" (*samyak*) specifically serves to distinguish it from false awakening; it clearly indicates that there are two meanings to "awakening" (*saṃbodhi*).

First, "awakening through discernment" (*saṃvedana-bodhi*) refers to the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), such as the four abodes of grasping, which are like thieves; only the noble ones (*ārya*) perceive them.

Second, "awakening through realization" (*pratibodha-bodhi*) refers to the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), such as ignorance (*avidyā*), which are like sleep; only the noble ones alone awaken to them.
Therefore, the remaining details are as explained below.

[Commentary: Since one intends to bestow eternal blessings upon all classes of beings, one should request the exposition of this sutra, desiring that those who have turned their backs on gratitude may all be able to repay their boundless debt.

[Commentary] The first phrase contains a subtle intention, suggesting that [the gift] will be eternal and long-lasting. "Xi" (錫) is glossed as "ci" (賜), meaning a bestowed gift; "zhonglei" (眾類) refers to the various classes of living beings.
For the filial son, this means distancing himself from evil and transforming toward goodness; for the two parents, it means departing from suffering and attaining joy.
Among all categories of beings, there are none who do not receive this bestowal, as the subsequent sutra states: "These are the Buddha’s disciples who cultivate filial piety and obedience."
Furthermore, it is said that this means causing all those who encounter difficulties to be free from sorrow and suffering. The next phrase establishes the teaching;
the Sage’s words were not uttered without a cause, for he preached this sutra in response to the request of Maudgalyāyana. The final two phrases demonstrate the intent of the teaching:
"those who turn their backs on kindness" refers generally to those in the world who are unfilial; indeed, anyone who has incurred a debt of gratitude toward others must [repay it].
If one knows how to repay the profound kindness of one's parents in raising and giving birth to one, yet as a Confucian fails to establish oneself and bring glory to the name,
or as one who has left the household life fails to uphold the precepts, cultivate the mind, and preach the Dharma to enlighten others—

these are all acts of unfiliality and constitute a total betrayal of that kindness. The very purpose for which this Teaching arose is precisely to encompass such individuals and enable them to repay their boundless debt of gratitude.
A verse from the *Shi* says: "Wishing to repay this virtue, the Great Heaven is boundless. This means that the kindness of one's parents is as vast as heaven, having no end.

[Commentary] May the various sages now silently bestow their grace upon what I have praised and recounted, so that for myself and others, whether living or dead, and whether separated from kin or dwelling together, we may forever be free from suffering.
Peace and Bliss.

[Commentary] The first phrase describes the composition of this commentary and praises its intent to assist the holy teachings; "narrating" (shu) refers to following the traces of the ancients to demonstrate humility.
The second phrase requests the bestowal of protection; having already expressed homage above, it now remains solely in... [the request for protection].
When the World-Honored One sought such protection, he prayed universally to all the sages; this included not only the Buddhas but encompassed the entirety of the Three Vehicles.

Regarding "subtle empowerment" (*mingjia*), the power of the sages is bestowed upon beings in both manifest and subtle ways. "Manifest" refers to directly beholding auspicious signs, such as being touched on the crown of the head or the emission of light.
"Subtle" refers to the latent influence of their efficacy, whereby one's goals are accomplished and tasks fulfilled. Out of respect for this, one does not presume to pray for a manifest response.
Therefore, I request your secret assistance. Gu Shan asked: "Since this sutra belongs to the Hīnayāna teachings, how can it speak of 'all Buddhas'?

The various sages do not contradict the "Small Vehicle" (Hīnayāna). Now, examining this response in detail, there are three points of error:
first, since the verse merely mentions "the various sages," how could it be restricted solely to the Buddhas? Second, the Dharmaguptaka school pays homage to the Buddhas;

because the doctrine of this school is consistent with the Mahāyāna, it begins by designating the Buddhas—how then can it be called the "Small Vehicle"? Third, [it relies on] the Great Teaching itself; how can it be called the Small Vehicle?

To permit discussion of the three types of Buddhas while asserting that this sutra’s general substance is entirely not of the Hīnayāna, yet failing to investigate the textual content and merely following old judgments to forcibly effect a reconciliation, leads the ignorant astray. May those of wisdom reflect deeply and avoid self-entanglement.

far-term, it involves liberation from the suffering of the two types of death to attain the bliss of Nirvana. Since antiquity, these three verses have been categorized into four sections:

Furthermore, it is said that while all treatises ultimately take refuge in the Three Jewels, one takes refuge here in the Buddha alone because the Dharma is the Buddha’s word and the Saṅgha are the Buddha’s children;
by mentioning the person, the teaching is encompassed, and by clarifying the father, the children are included.
Some say that these three verses correspond to the Three Jewels: the first verse, taking refuge in the Buddha, is self-evident; the second verse expounds the Sūtras...

3) the definitive determination of its central tenet; and 4) the formal explanation of the sutra text.

Regarding the interpretation: it may be that the first [section] concerns the object, the second the meaning, the third the practice, and the fourth the text; thus, the sequential interdependence of these elements is fully explained through analysis and exposition.
[Commentary]: The first section is further divided into four parts: (1) to repay past causes; (2) to respond to the present request;

[Commentary] Regarding the first point, repaying past causes: Prince Siddhārtha did not succeed to the royal throne but abandoned his kin and departed from his kingdom primarily to practice the Way and repay the kindness of his parents.

However, because the Bodhisattva’s intention was not to focus solely on himself, he established the *Ullambana* Dharma assembly to bestow blessings upon both his own and his parents’ kin. The original intent behind the emergence of this sutra is as follows:
This. [Commentary] The first section correctly elucidates this; the following concludes and indicates it. This section has two parts: first, recounting past causes;
then, clarifying the retribution received. "Siddhārtha" (悉達)—here translated as "Accomplishment of All Meanings"—is so named because he was the legitimate heir to King Śuddhodana.
The Crown Prince did not succeed to the royal throne because he grew weary of worldly glory; he abandoned his kin and left his kingdom, leaping over the city walls to enter the mountains.
Upon attaining the Way, he returned to his native land to enlighten his father, the King, and further ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to deliver his deceased mother.
Thus one knows that the fundamental purpose of practicing the Way is to repay one's parents.

[Commentary: Second, regarding the response to the present request: Mahāmaudgalyāyana, out of filial devotion born of his heart and wishing to deliver his parents to repay the kindness of their nursing, left the household life to practice the Path and became foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

He perceived that his deceased mother had fallen among the hungry ghosts (*preta*) and was unable to save herself; thus, he petitioned the Buddha for the Dharma and prepared an offering of a basin to rescue her from her inverted suspension.

Because he loved his parents and extended that compassion to all beings, he was requested by disciples, both monastic and lay, to entreat the Buddha to remain and leave behind this teaching for the sake of repaying Maudgalyāyana’s questions;
this is precisely the origin and purpose of the preaching of this sutra.
[Commentary] First, the primary section clearly elucidates the response to Maudgalyāyana; the following two sections summarize and indicate the preceding. Regarding the first:

it is a concise summary of the textual characteristics from beginning to end of this sutra, as will be explained by the author himself later, so there is no need for preliminary interpretation. The text is divided into three parts: first, the introductory section (*nidāna*);

second, the main body (*śarīra*), starting from "In saving oneself... and continuing below; third, the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*), starting from "Due to craving... and continuing below. This nature is inherently possessed and not derived from another.

Because it causes [this] to be so, it is said that the mind is the primary factor for greatness. The character "shī" (施) has a different pronunciation; its gloss is "yí" (移), meaning to extend or reach out to others.
[Commentary: Regarding the third section, which clarifies the Way of Filial Piety, there are further two parts. First, a general clarification that filial piety is the source of the two teachings.

[Commentary] Regarding the initial "general clarification":
[Record] It is called "general clarification" because it serves as a preliminary opening of the topical headings in contrast to the subsequent "specific similarities and differences."

[Commentary: To clarify that Confucianism takes filial piety as its foundation means that, beginning from the Son of Heaven down to the scholar-officials, the transmission of family and state has always involved the establishment of ancestral temples;
although the application of the five types of filial piety differs, the source of all virtuous conduct remains the same.

[Commentary] The initial heading refers to the following explanation. Based on the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety), the five ranks of honor encompass all under heaven, and it is evident that in Confucianism, filial piety is the fundamental principle. This text consists of two sections.

The first section specifically cites the ancestral temple to clarify that establishing temples and maintaining sacrifices is a matter of great importance for the state in honoring one’s ancestors; therefore, it is discussed first.

Citing this to clarify the fundamental meaning of the tradition passed down from state to state and family to family: "State" refers to the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords; "family" refers to the high ministers and commoners.
Those without ancestral temples maintain only four [generations]. According to the *Liji*, "Jifa" (The Law of Sacrifices): "The Son of Heaven establishes seven temples:

first, the father (*kao*); second, the grandfather (*wang-kao*); third, the great-grandfather (*huang-kao*); fourth, the eminent grandfather (*xian-kao*); fifth, the patriarchal grandfather (*zu-kao*)."

(The first ancestor is the progenitor; the five above receive monthly sacrifices, while the two below, who have been enshrined in the *tiāo*, receive seasonal sacrifices. When a temple becomes distant, it is designated as a *tiāo*; there are two *tiāo* (the *tiāo* temples are alternative names for the ancestral temples, specifically those of the Duke of Wen and the Duke of Wu;

because these remote ancestors performed meritorious deeds, their temples were specially retained and thus called *tiāo*). A feudal lord has five temples: the first is the father (*kǎo*), the second is the grandfather (*wáng kǎo*), the third is the great-grandfather (*huáng kǎo*)—all of whom receive monthly sacrifices;

the fourth is the current ruler (*xiǎn kǎo*), and the fifth is the great-great-grandfather (*zǔ kǎo*)—these four receive seasonal sacrifices. A high minister or Great Officer has three temples: the first is the father (*kǎo*), the second is the grandfather (*wáng kǎo*)... [and so on].

Regarding the sacrifices to the Three Augusts (all four seasonal sacrifices), the manifest father and the paternal grandfather have no ancestral temple (*miao*). For an *shi* (lower official), two temples are established: one for the father and one for the paternal great-grandfather (with four seasonal sacrifices);

the manifest father has no temple. For commoners, there are no temples. However, these rules are restricted to the ancestral system of the Zhou dynasty; thus, there were the two *tiao* (retired temples) of Wen and Wu.
If we rely on the *Book of Shang*, which states that "the ancestral temples of seven generations may be used to observe virtue," then we know the nature of the ancestral temple (*zongmiao*).
The universal principles since antiquity shall first present the general outline to dispel [misunderstandings] and entrust this written word to later students;
you must investigate the fundamental source without the trouble of extensively citing secular texts or recklessly engaging in forced interpretations.

Although the subsequent line generally explains the aspects of practice to clarify the distinct nature of the preceding phrase, the following phrase demonstrates the identity of the mind. As the *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "Love and respect reach their fulfillment in the performance of duties."

To apply the virtue of filial piety and instruction to the common people is the filial piety of the Son of Heaven. To act without danger or excess, long preserving wealth and honor, and being able to protect the altars of state and harmonize the people is the filial piety of the feudal lords.
To have clothing, speech, and conduct all conform to ritual regulations, and to be able to maintain the ancestral temple is the filial piety of the high ministers and great officers.
To love and respect one’s ruler and father, remaining loyal and obedient without fail, is [the filial piety of the common people].

The Duke of Zhou maintaining his ancestral sacrifices is the filial piety of an official; being careful of one’s person and frugal in expenditure to nourish one’s parents is the filial piety of a commoner.
This is what is meant by the distinction between the five types of filial piety. As for the "hundred practices," they are undertaken by taking up the general enumeration;
their source is the root itself.
[Commentary] Therefore, in the "Chapter on Opening the School and Clarifying the Meaning," it is designated as the essential path of supreme virtue;
the Way and its Power take this as their substance, and the teachings arise from it. How could a gentleman not strive for the root?

Since these are the eternal laws of heaven and earth, they must be made attainable through upward aspiration and downward compliance. Although it discusses the collapse of ritual and music, it ultimately rebukes those who wear brocade while eating coarse food.

*Rice*. [Commentary] The initial section, "Arriving and Growing," correctly demonstrates the fundamental meaning. The subsequent section, "How can there be...," clarifies that it must be practiced by humans.

The final section, "Although it is discussed...," clarifies that the matter cannot be abandoned. Within the first part, the "Chapter Opening the School and Clarifying the Meaning" is the opening chapter of the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety).
"Supreme Virtue and Essential Way" refers here to filial conduct; this cites the words with which Zhongni first instructed Zengzi, and is thus called the "heading.

The Sutra says: "The former kings (the Five Emperors and Three Kings) possessed Supreme Virtue (filial virtue, honored above all other deeds) and the Essential Way (the way of filiality, which subsumes the Five Constant Virtues), thereby bringing harmony to the world through their upward practice.
The people responded with concord, and there was no resentment between those above and below (through downward transformation). The following two sections concern the Way and its Virtue."

The preceding phrase of this section clarifies that the root of practice arises from its basis (the essence being the basis itself); the following phrase clarifies that the root of the teaching arises from it.

The Sūtra says: "Filial piety is the root of virtue" (the commentary adds the word "Way" [Dao] because of the preceding context), and "it is the source from which the teachings arise" (the former kings established words and transmitted instructions based on filial piety). The first two phrases of the next section are from the *Lunyu* (*Analects*), where it says:
The gentleman applies himself to the root—filial piety and fraternal duty. When the root is established, the Way arises (the Five Constant Virtues and a hundredfold conduct are thereby perfected).
Is not filial piety and fraternal duty indeed the root of benevolence (*ren*)? Benevolence is the foremost of the Five Constants, and filial piety is the fundamental practice of benevolence;

one knows that without filial piety, benevolence, righteousness, and moral virtue would have nothing upon which to rely. The latter phrase is derived from the *Classic of Filial Piety*. [This concludes] the Three Powers (*sancai*).
The *Zhangjing* says: "Filial piety is the constant of Heaven and the righteousness of Earth" (as explained above); it is the conduct of the people (for it is the root of virtue).
Since filial piety is thus the eternal law of Heaven and the natural advantage of the Earth, those born between Heaven and Earth ought certainly to take it as their model and put it into practice.
One must provide the following sentence from the *Liji*: therein, Zengzi said to Zisi (Zisi was the son of Boyu...)
Zi (the grandson of Confucius), Ji (Ji being the name of Zisi), said: "When I was observing the mourning rites for my parents, water and gruel did not enter my mouth for seven days.

Zisi said: "The former kings established the rites so that those who exceeded them would stoop to reach them (meaning the worthy, being able to exceed the standard, must lower themselves to conform), and those who did not reach them would stand on tiptoe to attain them (meaning ordinary people who do not reach it must strain upward to reach it; 'ti' means to look up; the modern character 'qi' has the same meaning). Therefore..."
"When a gentleman observes the mourning for his parents, he does not take water or grain into his mouth for three days.

This clarifies that the laws established by the former kings apply universally to both the worthy and the unworthy, so that all may understand the Way of Filial Piety without distinction among people.
The two sentences in the latter section both originate from the *Analects*. There, it says: Zai Wo (a disciple of Confucius) asked, "The three-year mourning period is already long enough."

"A period refers to a full year. The gentleman does not practice the rites for three years, and the rites will surely fall into ruin; he does not practice music for three years, and the music will surely collapse.
(This means that after a year has already passed, how much more so after three years—the fear is that the rites will be ruined and the music will collapse.

The Master said, "Would you feel at ease eating fine rice and wearing patterned silk? Zai Wo replied, "I would. The Master said, "If you feel at ease, then do it. However, a person of noble character..."
"When a son dwells in mourning, he does not find delicacies sweet (‘zhī’ means beautiful), he finds no joy in hearing music, and he finds no peace in his dwelling;

therefore, he does not do these things. Now you find peace in them, so you do them. (The repetition of the words indicates the depth of the reproach. Although it was Zai Wo who raised the question, Confucius ultimately rebuked him.
Thus, although Zai Wo was the one who asked, Confucius repeatedly censured him.
[Commentary: How profound! How great is filial piety! What could the virtue of the sages possibly surpass that of filial piety? [Record:
These three phrases are all from the opening line of the "Three Powers" (Sancai) chapter of the *Classic of Filial Piety*.

When Zengzi heard the five types of filial piety mentioned above, he was moved to such astonishment and sighs that he now employs those words to conclude the preceding text. The following two phrases are from the "Sage Governance" (Shengzhi) chapter.
The Sūtra says: "As for the virtue of the Sage, how could it exceed filial piety? (From this, it is evident that the Sage’s virtue cannot be further augmented.
[Commentary] Next, the teaching is explained as having filial piety as its foundation. Now, all Buddhas possess both the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Śākyamuni, in his transformation body, expounds the provisional teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings; Vairocana, in his true body, expounds the ultimate, real teaching.
The "Teachings" refer to the Sūtras and the Vinaya; the Sūtras elucidate wisdom and principle, while the Vinaya elucidates virtuous conduct.
[Commentary] The first phrase indicates the subject, and the following provides the explanation. The first two phrases present a general overview;

from "Śākyamuni" onwards, they specifically demonstrate the True Body (*dharmakāya*), which is the Retribution Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). If categorized by the three bodies, this includes the Dharma Body within the True Body; if discussed as four bodies, it refers to all four.
That is to say, the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) may be explained as being either distinct from or identical to the Response Body (sambhogakāya).

The "Birth" [Body] is the Response Body, while within the Dharma Body (dharmakāya), it contains the Retribution Body (vipākakāya), whether separated or combined, according to what is appropriate and without fixed limitation. Whether ancient or modern, their applications each rely on their own specific school;

there is no way to compare the similarities and differences of one's own school with others. These provisional teachings adapted to capacities encompass the entire period of the Buddha’s life, from the Deer Park to the Śāla Grove.

The *Jingjiujingshi jiao* (Teaching of Ultimate Reality) is restricted solely to the single division of the *Avataṃsaka*; however, this is merely according to the judgment of the Xianshou school alone.

(Gushan further includes the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, but these were spoken by the Nirmāṇakāya and thus still belong to the category of teachings adapted to specific capacities. *Śākyamuni* is fully called *Rocana* (盧舍那), which translates as "Full Purity.
"Full" means that the fruit is perfected; "Purity" means that all hindrances have been exhausted. Regarding "teaching," the following provides a general explanation of the term.
Regarding the provisional meanings of the teachings of Sūtra and Vinaya, each has its Great and Small [Vehicle] versions. The Sūtras can be understood accordingly;

the two divisions and five divisions of Vinaya belong to the Hīnayāna, while the *Śīlasamvara* and the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Necklace of Jewels) constitute the Mahāyāna Vinaya. The Sūtras of the True Teaching are exclusively Mahāyāna; the *Avataṃsaka* is the Mahāyāna Vinaya, and the *Brahmajāla* is the Vinaya of Principle and Wisdom.

Thus, principle and wisdom correspond to concentration and insight (*samādhi* and *prajñā*), while virtuous conduct corresponds to precepts and karma. This constitutes the two bodies of the True and Transformation [Buddhas].
If one examines both the provisional and ultimate teachings and finds that they both promote the Way of Filial Piety, then it is clear that the essence of the Śākya teaching is filial piety.
[Commentary] Therefore, when our Vairocana Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment, he immediately preached the Great Sūtra of the Avataṃsaka and the Great Precepts for Bodhisattvas.
Although these precepts encompass ten thousand practices, they take filial piety as their primary principle; thus, the initial heading states: "At that time, the Śākya..."
When the Buddha Kāśyapa Muni first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa:

the dharma of filial piety toward parents, teachers, and the Triple Gem, and of filial devotion to the Way of Ultimate Reality (which is likewise what the Sage Confucius called "the essential way of supreme virtue"). Filial piety is named the precept (*śīla*) and is also termed restraint (*saṃvara*).

[Commentary] Regarding the true body and the ultimate teaching, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is the foremost; regarding the transformation body and the provisional teaching, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is the final culmination.
Therefore, by citing the beginning and the end, all that lies in between is encompassed. The first section is divided into two parts;

first, the preliminary introduction concerning the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, which refers to the scripture as a whole, while "Bodhisattva Precepts" specifically refers to its very beginning. Thus, it is cited below.
The first part of the fourfold exposition indicates the teacher: it designates Śākyamuni as the subject of the transformation while inquiring about the true body of Vairocana.

This is explained for two reasons: first, because the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is transmitted from Vairocana; second, because Śākyamuni is identical to Vairocana. As the verse in the *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"Thus, the thousands of millions [of Buddhas] are the original body of Vairocana. Second, the location is indicated.
This refers to the tree beneath which one sits at the Bodhi-maṇḍa to attain the Way; thus it is called the "Tree of the Way" (also known as the "Tree of Awakening").

Regarding the attainment of the Way through the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), this refers to the realization of Perfect Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As for the Dharma established by the Four Departures, this refers to the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa*, which is translated here as "Individual Liberation.
Within this fourth category, there are further four parts: first, the designation of the name of what was established, which is the "Tree."
Second, the two factors that constitute the superior cause: namely, the three positions of filial piety toward one’s parents and so forth;

the six specific types of kindness—the kindness of parents who give birth and raise one, the kindness of teachers and the Sangha who provide the milk of the Dharma, and the kindness of the Triple Gem who deliver one from suffering; these are called the "heavy kindnesses.
As stated below, "All sentient beings of the six realms have been my parents," thus one must practice filial piety toward all universally. Third, the capacity [to repay].

Attaining the supreme fruit refers to reaching the Dharma of the Path (Note: This reconciles the terminology of Confucianism and Buddhism; the practice is the same while the designations differ). Fourth, the naming of the categories (the above divisions follow the Tiantai Commentary):
"Filial piety is named 'precepts'" because in the Bodhisattva precepts, there is nothing that does not accord with sentient beings, and all are acts of filial piety;
it is called "restraint" because one cuts off all evils toward sentient beings.
[Commentary: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "How marvelous! Our parents gave birth to us and underwent great suffering and affliction for a full ten months.
They bore us in their arms; after we were born, they pushed us toward the dry and placed us upon the damp, removing filth and attending to our excrement and urine.
They nursed us with milk and nurtured us, protecting our bodies. For these reasons, one must repay their kindness accordingly."

[He] makes offerings in accordance [with the truth]. [Commentary: The first part describes the debt of gratitude; from "By this" onwards, it exhorts [him] to repay it. Of these, the first three phrases provide a general indication of the fullness of suffering and affliction, while the subsequent section specifically enumerates the manifestations of suffering.
The *Ānanda-śāsana-sūtra* states that consciousness takes up residence in the mother’s womb for a total of thirty-eight weeks.
During each of these seven-day periods, a wind blows once every day to cause transformation (this is called "one rotation").
Calculating across thirty-eight seven-day periods, this totals two hundred and sixty-six days, forming nine months (as five are large and four are small, there is a deficiency of four days).
Furthermore, according to the *Pañcarājā-sūtra*, up until this point [the fetus] shares the same vital breath as its mother; after these four days, it is about to...
When the fetus is about to be born and its vital breath separates from that of the mother, it takes nine months and four days, extending into the tenth month;
thus, it is said to be "complete," referring to the fullness of the months. However, the duration of a person’s stay in the womb is not fixed:

for example, Rāhula experienced the suffering of birth after being in the womb for six years, the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila remained for sixty years, and Lǎndán (Laozi) stayed for eighty years; there are also cases of five or seven months.
Therefore, it is known that "ten months" is often used as a general expression.
[Commentary] The preceding section, which comprehensively clarifies that both teachings take filial piety as their foundation, is concluded.

[Commentary] Next, regarding the specific clarification of the similarities and differences in how the two teachings practice filial piety: within this, first the differences are clarified, and subsequently...
This reveals their commonality.

[Commentary] Although the two teachings differ in their outward manifestations (*vastu*), they are identical in their underlying intent (*citta*). Therefore, first clarifying their differences does not preclude their commonality;

subsequently, clarifying their commonality still requires seeing their differences. This serves to reveal the relative superiority of Confucianism and Buddhism, and to manifest the functional utility of each.
The depth of this [intention] is intended to cause those of the Confucian school to turn their hearts toward the Buddhist teachings;

thus it is so called. [Commentary]: The first refers to the difference in serving and nourishing [the parents] while they were alive; the latter refers to the difference in the remembrance and mourning after they have passed away.
[Commentary: As for the differences in the manner of serving and nourishing [one's parents], the Confucian tradition carefully protects the hair and skin to establish a name for future generations;
thus, when Zengzi was ill, he did not go out in springtime. The Buddhist teaching involves shaving the head and wearing torn robes, as the Dharma relies upon the present life;
thus, Udayana sent a letter to Qingzang to turn him away from heterodoxy. This is what is meant by "the ways of doing good differ, yet they all return to filial piety."
[Commentary] First, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation. This is further divided into two parts: first, the views of former scholars, and subsequently, the author’s own interpretation.
This pattern of dividing the text applies to all subsequent sections. Thus, the following provides a concluding indication of the Confucian school.

The first two phrases cite the *Classic of Filial Piety*, which states: "The body, hair, and skin are received from one's parents; not daring to damage or injure them is the beginning of filial piety. To establish one's character and conduct..."
To propagate one's name in later generations so as to bring glory to one’s parents is the ultimate fulfillment of filial piety. Regarding "Delighting in Spring," the *Liji* states:

Le Zheng Zichun (who served as the Director of Music and was named Zichun) descended from his hall and injured his foot; for several months he did not go out, yet he still wore an expression of sorrow.
His disciples asked him the reason, and he replied, "I heard this from Zengzi, and Zengzi heard it from..."
The Master said: "Of all that Heaven produces and Earth nourishes, none is greater than man.
When parents give birth to one in full integrity, the child returns to them in full integrity; this may be called filial piety.

Not to damage one's body and not to bring disgrace upon oneself—this may be called being complete in integrity. A gentleman, even in the space of a single step (qǐn), does not dare to forget filial piety."
For this reason, he had a look of sorrow. Zengzi opened his coverlet. The *Analects* says: "When Zengzi was ill, he summoned his disciples and said, 'Open my feet;

open my hands. (He opened the coverlet so they might see his body; 'coverlet' refers to the bedding. The *Shijing* says: 'Trembling and cautious, as if standing by a deep abyss, as if treading on thin ice.
From this day forward, I know I shall be spared [of injury]. (This means that as he was about to die, he knew he would be spared from further harm.)

Regarding the essence [of the teaching]: within the Śāsanā, "shaving the hair" (*zhù fà*)—where *zhù* is glossed as "to sever," meaning to cut off—and "wearing discolored robes" (*huài yī*) in the three colors of blue-black, madder, or saffron according to the Dharma, are so called because they are discolored from the objects [of ordinary life] and differ from the five directions and intermediate points of secular dress.

"Dharma-provision for the present life" refers to preaching the Dharma to awaken others and cause them to take refuge in the Triple Gem. As for *Udāyin*, it is found in the *Puyao jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra).
The Buddha told Udāyin (who was a disciple of the Buddha): "When I first left home, I made a vow to my parents that if I attained the Way of the Buddha, I would return to deliver them.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I must certainly return to my kingdom.

You should use your supernormal powers to manifest transformations in Kapilavastu so that they may believe that my body has already realized the Great Way. Udāyin, following this instruction, manifested many auspicious omens.
The father then believed that the fruits of the Buddha-way had been realized (this is what is meant by "communicating faith"). The King asked the Tathāgata when he would return to the kingdom;
Udāyin replied that he would come after seven days. The King was delighted and prepared the roads, while the entire nation looked up to him with joy.

Then the Buddha, leading the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, returned to the kingdom. Entering the palace, he accepted the King’s offerings, preached the Dharma to transform and guide him, and the King attained the Way.

Upon realizing the first fruit [of the path], all his kinsmen received the precepts (this account is said to demonstrate how the Tathāgata repaid the kindness of his kin, Udāyin; it is merely a transmission of the message).

*Jingzang* (Pure Treasury) turned away from heterodoxy; this refers to the wife of King Miaozhuangyan in the *Lotus Sūtra*, whose name was Jingde (Pure Virtue), who had two sons named Jingzang and Jingyan.
Their father believed in and followed the teachings of the non-Buddhist Brahmins, while the two sons manifested...

Through various miraculous transformations, the King’s mind was purified and he attained faith and understanding (that is to say, he turned away from heterodoxy). Together they went to the presence of the Buddha宿王華智 (Ratnakusumaguṇasāgaravairocana), where he resolved to attain bodhicitta.
That Buddha immediately bestowed upon the King a prediction that he would become a Buddha named 娑羅樹王 (Śālarājendra).
Thereupon, the King entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother and, together with his consort and two sons, left the household life to practice the Way. (The two sons...)
If one turns away from evil but has not yet left the household life, then the support for the Dharma comes first and the shaving of the head should follow.
In the *Shangshu* it is said: "Those who do good differ, yet they all return to order; those who do evil differ, yet they all return to chaos.
