[Commentary: There are three ways in which [the practices] differ after death. First, regarding the mourning period:

Confucians differ in their use of inner and outer coffins, burial sites, and the preservation of the physical form in the grave; Buddhists differ in their recitation of mantras, the performance of memorial feasts, and the offering of sustenance to assist the departing consciousness.

[Commentary]: "Coffin and outer casing" refers to the inner coffin that encloses the body and the outer casing that encloses the coffin. "Tomb site" refers to the burial pit; "establishing the tomb" means placing [the remains] within the grave.
"Preserving the form" means not allowing it to decay quickly. "Recitation" refers to chanting the names of Buddhas, sutras, and mantras.
"Posthumous vegetarian feast" refers to performing vegetarian rites in remembrance of the deceased. "Departure from consciousness" refers to the place where the spirit resides.
[Commentary]: Second, regarding the differences in fasting and memorial rites: the Confucians internally fast and externally fix their thoughts upon the deceased’s voice and appearance;
the Buddhists provide offerings and lecture on the sutras to support the karmic retribution of their deeds.

[Record]: Regarding "internally fasting" and so forth: whenever the Confucians wish to perform sacrifices, they first cultivate fasting and purification (*zhaijie*). As stated in the *Liji* (Book of Rites), "Sacrifice..."

The meaning is as follows: "One performs the inner fast (zhāi) within [the temple] for three days; because it is within the temple, it is called the 'inner fast. 'Inner' refers to the state of refined concentration. One performs the outer fast (zhāi) outside the temple for seven days;

because one stabilizes the mind in stillness and composure outside the temple, it is called the 'outer stabilization. On the day of the fast, one contemplates his dwelling place, his speech and laughter, his intentions, his pleasures, and his preferences—this is what is meant by 'visualizing his voice and countenance.
One prepares offerings, lectures on the sutras, and joins with others in recitation to offer posthumous prayers."

In observing the fasts, one should simply proceed with them and cultivate them according to one's capacity; it is not necessary to fixate rigidly on the karmic retribution regarding the place where one will be reborn.

[Commentary] Third, the lifelong differences from Confucianism: the Confucians slaughter living beings during the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—whereas the Buddhists observe restraint during three periods.

Releasing Living Beings (1. At the end of the year; 2. Upon the completion of the summer retreat; 3. On memorial days—whenever one’s means permit, one must release living beings on behalf of one’s parents for one *śaptāha* up to seven *śaptāhas*; this includes the first *śaptāha*, each subsequent *śaptāha*, the day of *sūtkṛta* [the cessation of wailing], the *śrāddha* days of *prathama-śrāddha* and *dvitīya-śrāddha*, and so forth;
however, nowadays this is generally done only upon the completion of three years). The Offering of the Alms Bowl for Precepts (*Śīla-pātra-pariṣad*; as described in this sutra...).

[Commentary] To briefly cite the four periods, one must also include the monthly sacrifices; "three nodes" refers to the three seasonal times. In the commentary, the first part indicates the three nodes according to one's capacity;
next, it instructs that one must perform [the rites] for one week up to seven weeks, taking the minimum as a baseline while more is virtuous.
The "first week" below clarifies the remaining times: the *zuku* (concluding wailing) is at the hundredth day, and the *xiang* (anniversary of death) is at the end of the year.
"Three years" refers to the period from now until the end of one's life; yet because this is not practiced in the world, it is said thus.
"Now, equal giving" refers to the precept of giving, which means receiving the precepts.

[Commentary: This is truly because the True Dharma has not yet arrived; for the time being, one must cause the mind to be bound [to virtue]—as in the saying, "when the love for ritual is gone, let the sheep remain"—and only now do we know the principle.
Having found a place of refuge, one should not continue to cling to provisional teachings.
[Commentary] To kill living beings for sacrifice to ancestors violates the teachings on benevolence;

yet, by wishing to cause Confucian scholars to all follow the Buddha’s words—not only so that those who have passed away may escape suffering and be reborn in heaven, but also so that those still living may cherish benevolence and receive blessings—the first section is truly authentic.

The essence [of our tradition] is Buddhism; since the Buddha appeared during the Zhou dynasty, his teachings were practiced in Western India, which is why it was said that they had not yet arrived here.

It was not until the Later Han dynasty that they first circulated in this land. As for the *Jifa* (Rituals of Sacrifice), although it originated in antiquity, it was drawn from the classical texts to be transmitted to the world;
thus, it attributes its origins to the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. However, both the Duke of Zhou and Confucius were great masters of expedient means who first established ritual laws so as to...
Only when people follow what is good can the Buddha’s transformation be easily propagated.

Since the seasonal sacrifices were not the original intent of the Sage, it is said that they merely serve to cause the mind to remain focused. The commentary cites the *Analects* to substantiate this provisional intention:

"Zi Gong wished to eliminate the sacrificial ox for the announcement of the month. (The "announcement of the month" refers to the monthly sacrifice; the living animal is called an "ox" [餼]. Since Duke Wen of Lu no longer personally attended the new moon ceremonies, Zi Gong wished to have Confucius abolish them.)

The Master said, "Ci (this is calling Subhūti by name), you cherish the sheep (pitying that his followers might die for it); I cherish the ritual (though the act itself may be improper, he wishes not to abolish the ritual of the 'announcement of the month').
These first two lines express the original intent of establishing the sacrifice; the latter two lines encourage abandoning Confucianism for Buddhism.
For those whose minds have found their refuge in principle, practices such as releasing living beings and bestowing precepts will surely enable them to uproot suffering."
Regarding provisional teachings: when comparing Confucianism and Buddhism, Confucianism is provisional while the Buddhist scriptures are all real.
Within Buddhism itself, there is a distinction between the provisional and the real, as clarified elsewhere.

[Commentary] Furthermore, among the greatest of blessings, none is greater than bestowing life upon sentient beings; this is the fundamental cause for becoming Brahmā or Śakra, and it is the Way of Heaven.
The earth possesses great virtue; to now slaughter that [creature] to sacrifice for this—how can this be close to a benevolent heart?
If this can be tolerated, what cannot be tolerated? Though it is said to seek blessings (the *Yueling* states: "In the middle energy of the ninth month, the sun is in the *Di* mansion;

order the officials to gather bundles of straw to nourish the sacrificial animals, even to the point of sacrificing to the spirits of the ancestral temple to pray for blessings for the people"), in reality, this is establishing enmity to pursue empty fame, bringing calamity upon the Way of the Gods (hence there are two classes of people on the road: those who sing and those who weep).

[Commentary] The first four lines describe the virtue of releasing living beings. The first two lines indicate the one who releases them—that is, one who does not kill the lives of creatures—and thus bestows life upon them.
The latter two lines explain that there is no merit like that of Brahmā and Śakra; when discussing virtue, how could it surpass Heaven and Earth?
These two [lines] fully enumerate the Three Powers (the three realms of existence) while simultaneously encompassing both teachings. When the Brahma King cultivates the Four Immeasurables, then...
Compassion is the foremost [of the four immeasurables] (the four equalities—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—are also called the Four Great Vows or the Four Immeasurable Minds).

When Śakra cultivates the ten wholesome paths, he places non-killing first (the ten wholesome paths consist of non-killing, non-stealing, and so forth). The *I Ching* says: "The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life" (Heaven and Earth take the production of life as their virtue).

It also says: "How great is the Primordial Qian! All things receive their beginning from it. Heaven provides the potential and Earth completes the formation; thus all things fully realize the principle of life.

The generation of boundless virtue is nothing greater than this. Next, we shall successively clarify the transgressions of killing. This section has two parts. First, we refute their violation of the Confucian tradition:

the Confucian school takes the extension of love to all things as the essence of benevolence (*ren*). Since you now kill the lives of others to sacrifice to your ancestors, you profoundly contradict the practice of benevolence.
If your conduct is not benevolent, then you are no longer gentlemen; such is the case for you and your peers.
This means that if one can still endure to commit such uncompassionate acts, what other matter could there be that is unbearable?

Although the subsequent passage rebukes his false attachments, the first sentence identifies the object of his attachment—the words regarding "seeking blessings" (*qífú*)—which originate from the *Yueling* (Monthly Ordinances) section of the *Liji* (Book of Rites).
The commentary notes that each month contains two solar terms (*qì*), and *Hànlu* (Dew Descends) corresponds to the ninth month.

The *jie* (limiting node) of *Shuangjiang* constitutes the middle month of the ninth lunar month (the "middle *qi*" among the two *qi* is called the *zhongqi*). The sun is in *Di*. This refers to the *taiyang* (Great Yang) reaching *Di*.

The "officers in charge" (*suoding yousi*) refers to the officials presiding over sacrifices. "To gather the *zhi-chu*"—*zhi-chu* means to collect grass. *Zhi-chu* refers to the sacrificial victims of pure color:
oxen, sheep, and pigs. [The text] omits the three intermediate phrases; as it says elsewhere, "to provide for [the sacrifice]."
The names of the Sovereign Heaven, the Supreme Deity, the great mountains and rivers, and the deities of the four quarters are listed;

the subsequent phrase clarifies that these are not the "Vimalakīrti" (Pure Name) [of the Buddha], for it says, "This is killing, this is the retribution for killing. The Buddha taught that the retribution of cause and effect does not deviate by even a hair’s breadth, hence it is called "real.
"Enmity" (*chóu*) refers to an adversary. The following two lines directly rebuke those who blindly follow [superstition]. "Empty fame" refers to seeking blessings through prayer.
Regarding the statement that "the Way of the Spirits is the numinous presence of one's ancestors," the commentary cites evidence from the *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Similes), which says:
"Five hundred hungry ghosts passed by dancing and singing, while five hundred good people passed by weeping. Someone asked the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"If the descendants of a hungry ghost perform meritorious deeds on its behalf, it shall attain liberation; therefore, they sing and dance."
The descendants of the deceased weep because they know that by continuing to practice killing, they will themselves undergo great suffering.

[Commentary] Question: If one's parents have been reborn in another realm, it is appropriate to change the sacrificial offerings to vegetarian meals (zhāi). But if they have fallen among the hungry ghosts (preta), would there not still be ancestral sacrifices (xiǎngsì)? Answer:

One should know that while millet and grain are not what provide the fragrance, water plants like *pín* and *fán* can be offered as substitutes; thus, the ritual of the *yào* sacrifice is superior [to mere slaughter].
If one kills an ox, how much more so for spirits and deities? Their ranks differ; how could they all receive the offerings?

[Commentary] In the question, it is argued that since those born into the realm of ghosts may accept sacrificial offerings, if one were to change the sacrifice, it would not be a sincere act of remembrance.

In the response, there are two parts: first, it clarifies that the essence of performing a sacrifice lies in sincerity, and thus it is appropriate to substitute meat with vegetarian offerings rather than necessarily killing an animal.

The first phrase of the citation is from the *Book of Documents*, where King Wu addresses Jun Chen (Jun Chen being the name of a minister), saying: "I have heard that when governance is perfected, its fragrance moves the divine intelligences;
it is not the millet and grain that constitute this fragrance, but rather the illustrious virtue alone that is fragrant" (for the spirits enjoy virtue and do not enjoy material offerings).

The second phrase is from the *Zuozhuan*, which states: "If there is sincere sincerity and clarity, then even the moss and weeds of mountain torrents, streams, ponds, and marshes—the *ping*, *fan*, and *yun* [types of aquatic plants]—"

The aquatic plants *ping* (duckweed), *fan* (mugwort), and *yun* (a plant with joints from which vegetables grow); the vessels such as the square basket (*kuang*), the round basket (*ju*), the tripod (*qi*), and the cauldron (*fu*)—the former being footless while the latter has feet;

and the water from stagnant pools (*huang*), ditches (*wu*), and runoff from roads (*lao*)—these may be offered to the spirits during sacrifices and presented to kings and dukes as delicacies. (The two following lines correspond to this. *Ping* is duckweed; *fan* is mugwort; *yun* is pronounced *wen*, a vegetable growing from its nodes; *zao* is aquatic algae. *Kuang* is square, *ju* is round; the *fu* is a cauldron without legs, while the *qi* is a tripod with legs.

*Huang* is pronounced *huang*; *wu* is pronounced *wu*, meaning stagnant water; *lao* is pronounced *lao*, meaning water flowing along tracks. They may be used for ancestral sacrifices (*ji si*) and may be served as offerings (*xiu*, meaning to present) to kings and princes. (This corresponds to the two subsequent lines.)

The *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) states: "In the east, the sacrifice of a slaughtered ox (referring to the lavish sacrifices of Zhou, the tyrant of Yin) is not as good as the *yuè* sacrifice of the neighbor to the west (King Wen, the Earl of Xi), which truly receives its blessing.

(This implies that because King Wen’s sacrifices were simple yet honored virtue, the elaborate was not equal to the frugal. Furthermore, since the realms of the spirits below differ according to their three grades and nine categories, it is not necessary that they all partake of offerings;
moreover, even using simple vegetables and plain food can manifest one's sincere heart. Below, this clarifies the three grades and nine categories.
Only the *bahudāna* (wealthy) pretas have food that can be eaten. Furthermore, the *Madhyamāgama* states:

"If, after death, those who perform sacrifices for others enter the realm of the hungry ghosts (*preta*), they obtain food; those in other destinies do not, because each has its own means of sustaining life.
(The term "realm-entering ghosts" [*rùchù guǐ*] refers to a specific class within the category of ghosts.)

[Commentary] Having finished explaining their differences above, there are two further parts next to reveal their similarities: first, explaining the similarity regarding their presence or absence; second, explaining the similarity regarding their transgressions and merits.
[Commentary] First, regarding the five phrases in the chapter on "Recording Filial Conduct," I shall distinguish their commonality, which encompasses both the period before death and after death.
[Sub-commentary] The chapter on "Recording Filial Conduct" refers to the tenth chapter of the *Xiaojing*; among its five phrases, the first three pertain to the period before death.
The latter two belong to what occurs after death.

[Commentary] One interpretation states: "In terms of dwelling together, one shows them respect; in the Confucian tradition, this is distinguished from the treatment of dogs and horses, while in the Buddhist tradition, one offers the entirety of one's seven-limbed body."

[Commentary] "Dwelling" refers to the time of ordinary life. Regarding the Confucian distinction between humans, dogs, and horses, the *Analects* states: "When Ziyou asked about filial piety, the Master said:
'The filial piety of the present age consists merely in being able to provide sustenance (the provision of clothing and food).

Now, even with dogs and horses, one can provide such sustenance; if there is no reverence, how does one distinguish [humans from animals]? (If one sustains one's parents without reverence, there is no way to distinguish this from sustaining other species. This is explained in the *Shìjìng*.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment and returned to his native land, King Śuddhodana prepared his carriage and went out to welcome him.

Upon seeing the Buddha, he prostrated; the Buddha then leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees (one *tāla* being seven *ren*, and one *ren* being seven feet—the total height is thus visible).

Having completed his prostration, he descended to the ground and inquired after the Buddha’s well-being. The Buddha, as the compassionate father of the world, was nevertheless still respectful toward his own kin.
One must not improperly accept gifts with the intention that others will follow this as a precedent.

[Commentary: Regarding the second point, "nurturing so as to bring about joy," for the Confucian, this refers to such practices as maintaining a pleasant tone of voice, lowering one's breath, and performing the rituals of warming the seat and checking on the bed.
For the Buddhist, it refers to the moderation of one's portion based on whether one is praised or reviled, and the sharing of one's robes and alms-bowl.
Because they are equal [in their compassion], there are such instances as [Prince] Sudāsa cutting his own flesh to satisfy his hunger.

[Commentary: In the *Qūlǐ* (Book of Etiquette) of the Confucian tradition, it says: "If one's parents have faults, one should admonish them with lowered breath and a cheerful voice. It further states:

"The ritual for being a son is to provide warmth in winter and coolness in summer" (*wēn* means to fan the bed; *qīng* is pronounced *qiàn*, meaning cool), and to settle them at dusk and... [the text continues].

"Morning inspection" (referring to inspecting the bedding and ensuring the dwelling is secure); thus, the following cites an event from the *Dongguan Hanji*, which states that Huang Xiang, as a filial and upright official (*xiaolian*), had no maidservants or attendants;

he personally undertook all manual labor, exerting his utmost strength to serve and nourish [his parents]. "In the heat, he fanned their bed and pillow; in the cold, he used his own body to warm their mat.
"Moderation" (*zhongjie*) refers to practicing economy and measure, that is, observing and assessing [one's resources]. "Belief and disbelieve" (*xinhui*) refers to faith and lack of faith.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one's parents do not have faith in the Triple Gem, one should provide them with a small amount; if they do have some faith, one may give them freely.

Regarding the reduction of robes and bowls, if it refers to the three robes and one bowl, there is no principle for giving these to laypeople. Alternatively, it may be a scribal error for "food and clothing" (*yishi*).
However, since people in the secular world today refer to the surplus property of the Sangha as "robes and bowls," it is possible that the author of the commentary followed common parlance.
This means that because one is impoverished, it is necessary to divide and reduce [one's own portion]; if one is already wealthy and sufficient, there is no need to force [others] to give.

If the gift is difficult to digest, it conversely becomes a burden and a source of transgression. Regarding the practice of cutting one's own flesh to satisfy hunger, the *Dà bàoen jīng* (Sutra on the Great Requital of Kindness) states:
"When Prince Susa’s parents were usurped by bandits and fled to a foreign land, they lost their way and ran out of food; [the prince] then cut his own flesh to provide for them."
The parents must cause [the child] to reach the path ahead.
[Commentary: Regarding the third point, "sickness brings about anxiety," in Confucianism, Emperor Wen once personally tasted the medicinal broth, and King Wu did not remove his crown or girdle;
in Buddhism, the Crown Prince used meat as medicine, and eminent monks carried it upon their own bodies.

[Commentary] Among the Confucian texts, the *Hanshu* states: "When the mother of Emperor Wen was ill for more than a year, Emperor Wen did not blink his eyes, did not remove his robes and cap, and would not take food or medicine until she had tasted them. The *Liji* states:
"When King Wen was ill, King Wu did not remove his robes and cap while nursing him; when King Wen ate once, he also ate once; when King Wen ate twice, he also ate twice."
After twelve days, he recovered from his illness (*jian* meaning "recovery from sickness"). The *Śākyamuni-dharmarāja-mahābhaiṣajya-sūtra* states:

When the parents of Prince Kṣānti were gravely ill, a physician declared that human flesh from a person who had never been angry was required as medicine. The prince thought to himself, "Since my birth, I have never been angry;
because of this, I am named Kṣānti (Endurance). This [flesh] may serve as the medicine. He further reflected that even if there were someone in the kingdom who had never been angry...

"How can I take that [meat] to save my kin? he thought, and so he cut his own flesh to serve as medicine; his illness was then cured (*chōu*). The *Biographies of the Tang Monks* states: "Daoji of the Northern Qi would always carry his books and scriptures on one shoulder and a pagoda image on the other, never shaming himself for such humble conduct. He once saw an old woman sweeping with a broom at the site of a Buddhist pagoda within the borders of Qi. He asked her why she was sweeping there, and she replied, "This pagoda has been here for many years, yet it has never been swept. Daoji then said, "I shall sweep it for you. When his mother passed away, he resigned his office to return home. His mother had a fondness for bamboo shoots (*sǔn*); whenever the season was right, Meng Zong would provide them for her.

After his mother’s death, approaching the winter solstice, he wished to offer bamboo shoots in sacrifice. He entered the bamboo grove and made a sorrowful appeal to Heaven and Earth, whereupon he was finally able to obtain some to present at the ancestral rites.
"Rice" refers to the story of Maudgalyāyana as cited below; "xiang" (餉) means to present an offering.

[Commentary: Since the ultimate teachings have not yet arrived, it is difficult to propagate [the truth of] retribution and response; therefore, for the time being, sacrificial rites are established so that people may pay reverence to the spirits.

[Commentary]: "The Supreme Teaching" refers to the Buddha-dharma; "retribution" refers to the causes and effects of the three periods of time. To say "provisionally established" indicates the meaning of expedient means (*upāya*).
[Sub-commentary]: "Spiritual efficacy" refers to the cognitive nature (*vijñāna*) of one's parents; this reveals that one's ancestors persist even after their physical forms have perished.
Since the spirit is not extinguished, how could this be a case of valuing the physical form while disparaging the spirit? The remainder is as previously analyzed.

[Commentary] The first two phrases reconcile differences with the preceding citation from the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*), which speaks of "the spirits of the four quarters" and "the numinous power of the ancestral temple.

Confucians claim that these spirits and numina are identical to the Buddhist notion of the nature of consciousness; thus, what is called "the non-extinction of the spirit" refers to the constant persistence of the conscious nature. The latter two... [text truncated]

If one were to reprimand Confucianism by saying that its emphasis on the physical form—such as serving the living, burying the dead, and performing ancestral sacrifices—is merely a matter of valuing the body and prioritizing the physical, while its claim to be "thin" regarding the spirit refers to a lack of solemnity in departing from consciousness;

then, if one follows the Buddhist teachings, one would be "thick" regarding the spirit and "thin" regarding the physical form. For the physical form is like withered wood and is not worth esteeming, whereas the spirit is what truly matters.

[Commentary]: Regarding those whose offenses are equal: in the Confucian system, one who transgresses the five punishments is subject to the five types of censure, yet such a person may not be included within the scope of an imperial amnesty.

In the Buddhist system, one whose name is inscribed among the seven heinous crimes (saptānantarya) is excluded from the precepts as a "seven-fold offender" (saptāvaraṇa), and their rebirth in the Avīci hell is certain.

[Commentary]: Among the Confucianists, the five ancient punishments were branding (marking the forehead), mutilation of the nose (the character *yì* is pronounced *yùqì*; it means cutting off the nose), castration (pronounced *fèi*; it means cutting off the feet), emasculation (for men;

for women, confinement), and capital punishment (pronounced *bì*; it means death). These are the five ancient punishments. The current five punishments are flogging, caning, penal servitude, banishment, and death.

Although the ancient and modern systems differ, the crimes of the "five rebellious acts" (*wǔ nì*) are not included among them; therefore, it is said that their categories transcend [those of] the *Xiào jīng*, which speaks of the five punishments.

These categories number three thousand, yet no crime is greater than filial impiety (meaning it lies outside the five punishments). Five [crimes] were punished by the "five chariots," wherein the five limbs were bound crosswise and torn apart.
The *Sanguo Chunqiu* states that Chitang, acting on his wife’s words, took his mother into the mountains and killed her;
when King Qin heard of this, he ordered her to be executed by the "five chariots," a punishment not covered by general amnesty.
Even if there were a general amnesty, these five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) would necessarily be excluded; by rule, they are not included in such pardons. "Amnesty" means to release.

Within the Hīnayāna of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the five heinous crimes are: killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

In the Mahāyāna, these are further increased by the killing of one’s Upādhyāya and Ācārya, which are termed the seven heinous crimes (as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: "killing a holy person" refers to killing...).

[They are] also Arhats. Regarding those who have been excluded from the precepts, this refers to persons who have committed the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*). Because the dharma of the precepts excludes and rejects them, they are collectively termed "obstructions to the precepts" (*śīlāvaraṇa*);

thus they are called the "seven prohibitions. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If there are those with the seven prohibitions, the teacher should not confer the precepts upon them; those without them may receive them.

The *Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha’s Physical Marks and Features* says that committing the heinous offenses constitutes the cause for the Avīci [Hell]. *Avīci* is translated here as "No-Interval" (or "Without Respite").
Regarding "Avīci" (Uninterrupted Hell): it is called "uninterrupted" because there is not even a momentary interval of pleasure.

Furthermore, when a single person falls into this hell alone, their body pervades the space between the hells such that no empty space remains; the hell extends eighty thousand *yojanas* in all four directions, penetrating through to its core, and the body is equal in size to the hell itself, yet they do not obstruct one another.

[Commentary]: Regarding those whose merit is equal: for Confucians, it is manifested at their gate and village; for Buddhists, it is polished through the virtue of the precepts and serves as the cause for the Pure Land (as stated in the *Amitābha Sūtra*:

"One should cultivate the three types of merit," beginning with filial piety toward one's parents, up to these three kinds of karma being the direct causes for the Pure Lands of the Buddhas of the three periods).

[Commentary]: In the Confucian states, whenever there is one who practices filial piety within a prefecture or county, the government immediately grants them the "Floral Banner" (jìngbiǎo) and displays it upon their gate.

This is also intended as an encouragement and reward. Regarding the retribution from Heaven: when comparing Buddhism and Confucianism, if one practices filial piety with utmost sincerity, one will certainly attain birth in the heavens;

To claim that [the teachings] are for the sake of retribution from the heavens above, rather than being a response to those below, is somewhat remote from the meaning of the Buddhist doctrine. Regarding the clarification of the purity of preceptual virtue (*śīla-guṇa*):

[Commentary: It is like a person in the world who desires that the five grains within their granaries be abundant and never lacking from year to year.

[Commentary: The analogy can be understood through this. The five grains refer to hemp, millet, broomcorn millet, wheat, and beans.
[Commentary: It is the same within the Dharma: one takes compassion, reverence, and filial piety as the seed;
food, clothing, wealth, and even one’s own life as the ox and the plow; and the impoverished, the sick, the Three Jewels, and one’s parents as the field.

[Commentary]: Compassionate mind is directed toward the field of pity consisting of the poor and the sick; a respectful mind is directed toward the field of reverence consisting of the Three Jewels below; filial mind is directed toward the field of parental kindness below.
Material wealth such as food and clothing constitutes external wealth, while one's own body and life constitute internal wealth.

[Commentary]: If a disciple of the Buddha wishes to obtain the inexhaustible, life-after-life manifestation of the hundred-fold adornments within the *ālayavijñāna*, they must exercise compassion, reverence, and filial piety to respectfully provide clothing, food, wealth, and even their own lives to support those who are poor or ill, as well as the Three Jewels and their parents;
this is called "planting merit. If one does not plant [merit], one will remain impoverished and devoid of merit and wisdom.
The perilous path of birth and death is called the field for planting merit; it is named a "field of merit" (puṇyakṣetra) because it is like a field for sowing grain.

[Commentary] The disciples of the Buddha correspond to the worldlings above, while the *ālayavijñāna* corresponds to the granaries and so forth below. One must transport the lower to correspond with the upper, taking the seeds and so forth;
one does not take the lower to correspond with the upper by exhausting it entirely. This means that the lower illustrates the names, while the upper refers to the three fields.

One may plant merit; thus it is universally termed the "Field of Merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*). The name "Field of Merit" is raised here as a combination of both the Dharma and its metaphorical illustration.

[Commentary: Now, seeds may be potent and fresh, or parched and withered; fields may be fertile and rich, or hard and barren. Likewise, there are differences in the intensity of one's compassionate, respectful, and filial mind—whether earnest and sincere or indifferent and lax;
in the depth of poverty; in the severity of illness; and in the nature of the Buddha—whether he is the True Buddha or an Emanation Buddha.

There are those who abide in the world and those who enter extinction; there are the Small and Great Teachings; there are the provisional and the real; there are the Sangha who uphold and those who violate [the precepts];
and there are parents who give birth—each of these seven generations is clearly visible when matched against the fields of merit, whether they be fertile or barren.
[Commentary] First, the analogy is presented: "emaciated and thin" refers to barren soil, as in the following correspondence with the Dharma. First, "seed" corresponds [to the practitioner's state]:

earnestness is like fresh and fertile [soil], while negligence is like parched and withered [soil]. Second, "poverty and lowliness" corresponds to the field [of merit]. There are three [types of fields]; first, the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*):

shallow and slight [merit] is like the emaciated, while deep and heavy [merit] is like the fertile. From "the Buddha" downward corresponds to the field of respect (*guru-kṣetra*); the Buddha is the true [field].
Abiding is considered "fat" while cessation is "lean. Conventionally, the small is lean and the real, great is fat.
Regarding the Sangha, violating the precepts is lean and upholding them is fat. For parents, being of low status is lean, while being born into a field of gratitude (en-sthāna) is fat;
for seven generations, such status is lean.
[Commentary: Now, because this *Ullambana* assembly possesses three kinds of "fertile fields," it is called "superior. That is to say:

[Commentary]: Second is the Vinaya, which is translated here as "Discipline" (Tiaofu). "Discipline" (*tiao*) refers to refining the three types of action (*trikarma*); "subduing" (*fu*) refers to restraining transgressions and faults.
This teaching elucidates the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).

[Commentary] The translations of the name and explanations of its meaning are all based on a single perspective. It is also called *vinaya*, *vinīta*, and so forth. The ancient translation was "extinction" (*mie*); the correct translation is "discipline" (*lü*).

"Disciplining" (*tiaoliàn*) means "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*). This refers to the practice of "active observance" (*zuòchí*), which involves subduing and restraining oneself to remain free from transgressions; this is the practice of "passive observance" (*zhǐchí*).
[Commentary]: The three types of Abhidharma are here translated as "Dharma-in-Relation-to" (Duifa). "Dharma" refers to *nirvāṇa* and the Four Truths;

"in relation to" (*pratya*) means to be directed toward or to contemplate. That which performs this relating is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). This teaching elucidates the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
[Commentary] The initial translation of the name is also called *Abhidharma-dharma*. "Nirvana" refers to the fruit toward which one is headed;

the "Four Truths" refer to the principles that are the objects of contemplation. Both of these belong to the category of "objects. "Facing toward" (*prati*) corresponds to Nirvana, and "contemplating" (*dharma*) corresponds to the Four Truths;

[Commentary] However, the Sūtras are the Teaching of Transformation (*vyavahāra-śāsana*), which opens the way for and guides sentient beings; the Vinaya is the Teaching of Regulation (*niyama-śāsana*), which restrains and governs their conduct;
and the Śāstras are those that investigate, analyze, and provide explanations.

[Recorded Notes] "Opening the way for and guiding" means merely opening the path for faith and understanding, allowing things to proceed according to the capacities of beings, whether they comply or not. "Restraining and governing conduct" means...

[Commentary]: The "Five Vehicles" (pañca-yāna) are so named because they serve as conveyances for transport. The five refer to the vehicles of humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
These five possess varying degrees of power, and thus their capacity for transport varies in both magnitude and distance.

[Commentary] First, the names are shown; below, the ranks are listed. The Vehicle of Humans has little power and carries one a short distance; the Bodhisattva Vehicle has great power and carries one a long distance.
Regarding the three intermediate vehicles, compared to what precedes them they are great and distant, but compared to what follows them they are small and near.
As for the Bodhisattva Vehicle, it is called the Buddha Vehicle from the perspective of its cause, and is designated by the name of its fruit.
[Commentary: The vehicle for a single person refers to the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, which transport sentient beings across the three miserable realms to be born into the human path;
it is like a small boat crossing a mountain stream.
[Commentary] First, the heading; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there is first the Dharma and subsequently the analogy. Regarding the Dharma, there are three parts:

the vehicle upon which one mounts, the realm to be transcended, and the retribution to be realized—the latter three examples are divided accordingly. Taking refuge means following a teacher to perform the ritual of taking refuge in the Triple Gem. The five precepts are:
not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not lying, and not drinking intoxicants. As soon as...
This is a brief explanation.

[Commentary]: The "two celestial vehicles" refer to the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths of action and the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, which transport sentient beings across the four continents and reach the higher realms, respectively like a boat crossing small rivers and large streams.

[Commentary]: The ten wholesome paths of action are divided into three grades: practicing them in the lower grade leads to birth as an asura; the middle grade leads to birth as a human; and the upper grade leads to birth among the gods of the desire realm.

The four dhyānas are mentioned separately because the form realm (rūpadhātu) is distinct from the higher realms. The eight meditative absorptions (aṣṭa-samāpatti) collectively comprise both the form and formless realms, as they are all "immovable karma" (āneñjya-karma).
The four continents and the lower levels of the desire realm are the states to be transcended; the higher realms generally refer to the three heavens [of the form realm].

Regarding the retributions thus experienced: if one discusses them according to what is transcended, the ten wholesome actions transcend the four continents; the four dhyānas transcend the desire realm;
and the four formless attainments transcend the form realm. [Commentary]:
Third, the Śrāvaka vehicle refers to the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths; fourth, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle refers to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
All these Dharma-gates transport sentient beings across the three realms to reach the nirvana with remainder and without remainder, enabling them to become arhats and pratyekabuddhas;
they are all like great ships that cross over vast rivers and streams.

[Commentary]: Although the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas differ, there is no distinction between that which is transcended and that which is reached; therefore, they are explained together.

When the fetters and delusions are exhausted, if one remains with a physical body, it is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa with remainder). When the body is consumed by the fire of transformation and both body and wisdom cease to exist, it is called *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvāṇa without remainder).
[Commentary: The fifth is the Bodhisattva Vehicle, which refers to the dharma-gates of compassion, wisdom, and the six perfections that transport sentient beings,
enabling them to collectively transcend the realms of the three vehicles and reach the other shore of unsurpassed bodhi and great parinirvāṇa,
like crossing the ocean by ship.

[Commentary] Because he descends to transform those below, there is compassion (*karuṇā*); because he seeks upward, there is wisdom (*prajñā*). Generosity, morality, diligence, patience, meditation, and wisdom constitute the six practices;

because practicing these six dharmas enables one to reach the other shore, they are called the "six perfections" (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). To transcend the three realms is to exit the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence);

to transcend the three vehicles is to exit the *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence). *Bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* refer to the fruit of Buddhahood. *Bodhi* is translated as "awakening" (*jue*), which distinguishes it from that of the two vehicles.
Because the self-awakened bodhisattvas have not yet reached fulfillment, it is called "unsurpassed"; *nirvāṇa* is translated as "quiescent extinction.
To distinguish it from the preceding Hīnayāna, it is called "Great" (*mahā*). "Ship" (*pō*) refers to a large vessel.
[Commentary: This present sutra is subsumed under the vehicle of humans and devas, and is contained within the Hīnayāna Piṭaka.
[Commentary] Guifeng’s classification and interpretation follows the Xianshou school, which establishes two types of Hīnayāna: first, those of humans and devas; second, those of the Two Vehicles.
This sutra is not yet Hīnayāna itself, but it is merely subsumed under the category of Hīnayāna.

Now one should ask: on what basis is this sutra thus classified? (Gushan says: "This is spoken in terms of the beings to be saved. If it is argued that [the classification is based on] Maudgalyāyana’s mother being liberated...

Regarding the statement that one is born in the heavens yet referred to as a "human and celestial being" (nradeva): furthermore, even Maudgalyāyana’s mother was merely born in the heavens; how could she be said to encompass both humans and celestials?
Moreover, the expression "born in the heavens" appears throughout the Mahāyāna sūtras. For instance, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"By copying this sūtra, at the end of one's life, one shall be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; by upholding, reciting, and chanting it, one shall immediately go to the Tuṣita Heaven," and so forth. Furthermore, the *Brahma...* [sūtra]...
The *Wangyun* states: "Explaining and preaching the Bodhisattva precepts provides merit for the deceased to be reborn among humans or in the heavens. It further states:

"Those who receive and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts will constantly be born among humans or in the heavens. Does this not mean that these should all belong to the teachings of humans and devas (*manuṣya-deva*)?
Moreover, since the practices and fruits of the two vehicles of humans and devas explained above are entirely distinct, how can they be conflated into one and referred to as "humans"?
Since it is said that the teachings must be categorized by the heavens, one must determine their ultimate destination; to what category does this sutra ultimately belong?
Furthermore, within the exposition of filial piety, the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* Sūtras are cited to clarify that the Buddha’s teaching takes filial piety as its foundation.

Since these are cited as the perfect, sudden, ultimate, and definitive meanings to demonstrate filial piety, how can the classification of the teachings be restricted merely to the human and celestial realms? Moreover, to what [category] does it belong?

The verse of homage states: "Through many kalpas of repaying parental kindness, one accumulates causes to achieve perfect enlightenment. This clearly demonstrates that filial conduct is profound and that one has penetrated the Buddha Vehicle.
Yet, when analyzing the sūtras, it is said that [the recipients of this homage] are merely humans and devas; is this not a contradiction between the earlier and later statements?

Furthermore, in the *Gushan Ji* (Records of Mount Gu), while explaining the verse of homage, it clarifies that the Three Jewels of the same essence are the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). How can these two accounts be reconciled?
Within this, there is the meaning of awakening, comprehension, guiding, sustaining, and harmonization.

Furthermore, it explains that being free from suffering and attaining peace and bliss refers to obtaining the bliss of the four virtues of unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvana: permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Moreover, it explains that the "accomplishment of the master" means that delusion is realized as the True, and thus the false is Bodhi; therefore, awakening is itself the realization of the false.

Furthermore, since true afflictions are themselves bodhi, and since the explanation that the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is itself the true ripening of the eight consciousnesses and so forth employs Mahāyāna terminology to interpret the preceding passages,
it would be inappropriate to categorize these as the Hinayana teachings of humans and devas. Conversely,
if one were to judge this sutra according to the Hinayana teachings of humans and devas, then it would be inappropriate to employ Mahāyāna terminology.

The *Yishu* (Exegesis of Meaning) further explains the preceding passages regarding the provisional manifestations of the great beings of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), stating that they are identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in "internally concealing their bodhisattva nature while externally manifesting as śrāvakas. It then poses its own question: "What distinguishes this present sutra from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?

Since this sutra is judged to belong to the level of humans and devas (*manuṣya-deva*), how can one compare it with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to determine their similarities and differences? From this, one knows [the intent of] the commentary.

The records of our school’s traditions have become confused, and their origins and details have diverged through errors; for generations alike have been deluded, failing to investigate the essential substance.

Furthermore, while the teachings for humans and devas are intended only for those of the most dull faculties—allowing them to escape the three miserable realms and receive the Way—they do not exempt them from birth and death, which is certainly not the Buddha’s fundamental intention.
Therefore, among the Four Teachings of Tiantai, the teaching for humans and devas is not included. As for Nanshan [Zongmi], he likewise did not list it.
The two commentaries state that the precepts were established solely for the sake of the Noble Path, and were not originally intended as worldly merit for gods, lords, or kings.

If these teachings had been promulgated merely for such secular purposes, the Buddha would have taught them as being equivalent to those of ordinary people; therefore, one must seek the ancestral instructions and profoundly investigate the Buddha’s intent.
This demonstrates that he did not merely master a single sutra, but rather thoroughly understood the Great Transformation. Now, let us examine this in detail.

Within the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), it definitely belongs to the Sūtra Basket and is included among the teachings of transformation; within the Five Vehicles, it definitely belongs to the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna.
However, in general discussions of doctrinal classification, one must first examine the nature of the practice expounded in the primary teaching;

second, investigate the depth of the benefit derived by the audience who heard it; and third, seek the relative excellence of the textual meaning and its underlying intent. This constitutes the first [criterion].
The primary benefit of this sutra lies in its efficacy in benefiting all beings; its text is the very embodiment of the function of the expressive medium.
By means of this distinction, there is nowhere it does not penetrate. First, regarding the practitioner: if we discuss filial conduct in general, there are many paths.

If one follows the Confucian school and practices pure filiality toward one’s parents, this is merely a worldly retribution, a practice leading to the realms of humans and devas. If, however, one is like Maudgalyāyana...
To personally cultivate the path and achieve the fruit of Arhatship is the practice of the Śrāvaka of the Hīnayāna.
If one follows the previous citations from the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra*, these are all the Mahāyāna practices of a Bodhisattva.

However, the present context is specifically restricted to this sūtra alone, which focuses exclusively on the Mahāyāna practice; this is because on the day of the Pravarana (Self-Indulgence), one makes offerings to repay one's debt of gratitude in a single movement of mind.

Truly, whether one possesses both self-power and other-power, or whether such power exists or not, regardless of whether it pertains to oneself or others, to pity sentient beings, to exhaust one's wealth, and to uproot suffering while bestowing joy—since this is no minor practice, it must be attributed to the Mahāyāna. Thus, a sutra says:

"I shall now proclaim the Dharma of salvation, so that all who are in distress may be freed from sorrow and suffering. Furthermore, the term "all" universally encompasses the entire realm of living beings.
How could it stop at the words that my own kin have transcended suffering and surpassed the two deaths? It is not merely the realm of ghosts;
as the Brahmajāla Sūtra states, "All sentient beings have been my parents.

Since I have been born from them in every lifetime, this accords with what was previously called "repaying kindness through successive kalpas" and "accumulating causes to attain Buddhahood. Based on such clear evidence, how can one doubt the Great Teaching?

Second, clarifying the conclusion and benefit (*anuśaṃsa*): This refers to the sūtra author concluding and indicating that the assembly of those who heard [the teaching] attained awakening and realization;
thus it is called "concluding the benefit. It does not mean referring specifically to the individuals being saved, as the sūtra says:

"The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the great assembly of bodhisattvas were all greatly rejoiced. If they were merely minor practitioners, devas, humans, or those with ordinary merit, how could they have been "greatly" so?

When the assembly of bodhisattvas heard this, they all rejoiced; since "rejoicing" implies awakening and the further development of the great resolve (*mahācitta*), the text below cites the *Enzhong jing* (Sutra on the Weight of Gratitude) to conclude the benefits, stating: "That Śakra and the various devas developed the bodhicitta—is this not clear evidence?
That sutra further states: "If sons or daughters of good family can, for the sake of their parents, uphold this Mahāyāna..."
A single phrase, a single verse, or a single sutra of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā causes even the grave sins of the five heinous crimes to be completely extinguished when they reach the ears or eyes.
Second, although the two sutras are of a similar nature, that one clearly designates itself as Mahāyāna, so there is no doubt about it.

Third, regarding the meaning of the text: first, the text showing the progression as demonstrated above; second, the text concluding with the benefits mentioned previously; third, the assembly of those who heard [the teaching] together.

There is a Great Bodhisattva who, among the four classes of monastics receiving offerings, manifests through the provisional transformations of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) within the Small Vehicle teachings to discourse upon the ten stages, thereby demonstrating his skillful means (*upāya*).
Master Shengwu of Wuzhi judged this to belong to the Mahāyāna, which deeply accords with the intent of the scriptures;
yet, in the *Gushan ji*, he abruptly dismissed it as erroneous. To wield the pen to transmit instruction with such casualness is indeed reckless.
If this is so, why does this sūtra alone—among the various sūtras of the *yīdài* (one lifetime) period as judged in the catalogs—receive such singular censure?

(As for those in ancient catalogs who judged it to be a Hīnayāna text, they have already been refuted by Master Sheng. Since many people cling to their attachments and disputes, I cannot avoid prolixity; yet, fortunately, one should rely on the Dharma rather than on persons.
Have you not heard that when one encounters the meaning, one must follow it? My only concern is that the sublime teaching may be submerged and future generations stifled.

I shall attempt to provide a critical analysis. [Commentary] Regarding the third section, "Discriminating to Establish the Fundamental Tenet": The fundamental tenet of this sutra is the offering of filial piety and obedience to rescue others from suffering and repay their kindness.
Now, I shall distinguish this through two gates: first, explaining the characteristics of the practice; second, correlating the numerical categories of the phrases.
[Commentary] Generally speaking, there are four [aspects]: filial piety is the mind, making offerings is the practice, relieving suffering is the merit, and repaying kindness is the function.
Now, examining the core tenet (*mūla-artha*) of this sutra, the tenet is the meaning; since a country cannot have two sovereigns, how could there be four?
Therefore, we establish "repaying kindness" as the tenet, while the other three are naturally subsumed within it. The opening of the sutra text states: "I wish to repay my parents."

The kindness of nursing and suckling is the first proof. Furthermore, the Commentary cites three translations, where the title of the third is established as the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Repaying Kindness);
this is the second proof. Students should understand that these are explained according to the Commentary.

[Commentary]: "Initial" refers to Maudgalyāyana’s original intent to repay his filial piety and gratitude through his spiritual power; however, as this was beyond his reach, he first entered the monastic life.
Thus, having attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), he immediately contemplated the three realms and perceived that his deceased mother had been reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

(The fact that those who have attained the Way do not necessarily do so solely for the sake of their parents serves as proof that Maudgalyāyana entered the monastic life specifically to repay his debt of gratitude. Although he sent her fragrant food, it turned back into [filth] as soon as it reached her.

Lamenting piteously amidst a raging fire, he threw himself before the Buddha and followed his instructions to prepare an offering basin; by bathing his body in it, he was liberated from the suffering of one kalpa.
Thus, the great repayment for the labors of those who gave him life and nurtured him is fully detailed within the essential tenets of this sutra through these four meanings.

[Commentary] The first section describes filial piety; the sub-commentary (*zhùwén*) provides clarification to dispel doubts, for there may be concern that all sages enter the Path because of their parents, and thus they are able to begin contemplation immediately.
Hence it says, "to verify this. The section beginning with "although" (雖) describes the offering of provisions; the character "xuán" (旋) is pronounced level-tone (píngshēng), meaning "to seek" (xún).

The section beginning with "extracting" (拔) describes the removal of suffering; the section beginning with "not inferior" (不下) describes the repayment of kindness. The final two lines provide a summary.
[Commentary] Second, regarding the enumeration of the phrases, there are four sets of four phrases.

[Commentary] First, the two characters "filial" (xiào) and "obedient" (shùn) themselves constitute four phrases: 1. Filial but not obedient, such as providing the nourishment of the three sacrificial animals;
2. Obedient but not filial, such as when one is ill and requests forbidden food, and one immediately provides it when the desire arises.
Not admonishing regarding matters that ought not to be done—these three cases constitute both filiality and obedience, characterized as "concealment without offense.

Admonishing three times and then following along, observing the countenance and discerning the intent, such that no changes are made for three years, constitutes both filiality and obedience. Conversely, there are four instances that are neither filial nor obedient, such as the case of burying one's father in water.
[Commentary] The first sentence [of this section] cites the *Classic of Filial Piety*: "When occupying a high position, do not be arrogant; when serving as a subordinate, do not cause disorder;

when among the multitude, do not contend. (The term "multitude" [醜] refers to the crowd. "If one is arrogant while occupying a high position, they will perish; if one causes disorder while serving as a subordinate, they will be punished;

if one contends while among the multitude, there will be conflict" (conflict refers to armed strife). "If these three failings are not eliminated, then even if one provides the nourishment of the three sacrificial animals daily, it still constitutes unfiliality."

(That which was previously called unfilial is now called filial; it is so called because it is not a failure to provide sustenance, yet one cannot be said to be compliant because one fails to cultivate oneself.

Regarding the second point, providing offerings at memorial services while failing to remonstrate against what is evil is compliance rather than love for one’s parents, and thus is not filial piety. The *Classic of Filial Piety* states:

"If a father has a son who remonstrates with him, his person will not fall into unrighteousness. Therefore, when confronted by unrighteousness, one must remonstrate; how can one follow the father's commands otherwise?

Regarding whether this constitutes filial piety, the third sentence refers to the *Book of Rites*, which states: "In serving one's parents, there should be concealment of faults but no offense; (one should conceal their transgressions and offer gentle admonitions without offending their countenance).
In serving one's ruler, there should be offense but no concealment; (one should offend their countenance and speak directly, stating their merits and shortcomings).

In serving one's teacher, there should be neither offense nor concealment; (though one does not offend their countenance, one speaks of their merits and shortcomings). Serving parents is based on affection (*en*); serving a ruler is based on righteousness (*yi*); serving a teacher lies between affection and righteousness. As for the practice of "three admonitions," the *Book of Rites* says: "If [the parent] follows after the third admonition..."
In serving one's parents, if after three admonitions they do not listen, one should follow them while weeping aloud.

Regarding "following their countenance," the *Analects* records that when Zi Xia asked about filial piety, the Master said, "The countenance is difficult. The commentary notes that "to receive and follow the expression of their countenance" is what is truly difficult.
Regarding "observing their will," the *Book of Rites*, in the section on Zengzi, states: "What is called filial piety by the gentleman means to anticipate their intentions and comply with them..."

"Respecting the Will: On Filial Piety toward Parents" (This refers to a son observing his father’s will; it accords with the general meaning of the text and is consistent with the *Analects*, though the phrasing differs slightly. after his death, observe his conduct. If for three years one does not alter the way of the father, he may be called filial. 4. Zhongshi Chuan Kunzi (some editions read Hunzi).
When his father was being water-buried in the Kunming Pond, the son was unfilial and frequently disobeyed him;
his father ordered that he be cast into the water, intending for him to be buried in the earth, yet the son specifically complied with this, whereas the opposite would have been disobedient.

[Commentary]: Second, regarding filial piety (*kṣānti*) and the making of offerings (*pūjā*), there are four permutations: first, filial piety that is not the making of offerings, such as [the cases of] Dong An and Wang Xiang;
second, the making of offerings that is not filial piety, such as practicing the rectification of the family for one's own sake to seek merit;
third, both being present, namely the *Ullambana* Assembly; and fourth, neither being present, which refers to those who are rebellious and stingy.
[Commentary] The first sentence refers to the *Xiaode zhuan* (Biographies of Filial Virtue), which states that Dong An was a native of Kuaiji (the stele identifies him as a native of Quzhang).

He lost his father at a young age and raised his mother, serving her countenance and bringing her joy. Although he was poor, he fulfilled his filial duties; although his neighbor was wealthy, he was haggard with worry because he harbored an evil nature that constantly caused his mother anxiety.
Upon learning of this, the neighbor became enraged; waiting for Dong An to be away, he struck his mother. The mother then informed Dong An.

His resentment deepened until his mother’s death; once the burial was completed (referring to the end of the three-year mourning period at Lu’s grave), he killed a neighbor and presented the head to him, saying:

"My mother knew that while you were first in charge of her care, now that her care has ended, I have settled my vengeance. He then threw himself upon the authorities to confess his crime, but he was pardoned during a general amnesty.
Wang Xiang’s mother was fond of fish; when the ice was thick and frozen, Xiang lay down upon the ice and obtained fish to serve her.

Regarding the third [verse], the phrase "both" (*ubhaya*) refers to the *Ullambana* [Sūtra] in order to distinguish it from the core tenet of that scripture; the same applies to the following two cases.

Following the previous example, the single phrase "filial and compliant" (*kṣānti-śuśrūṣā*) subsumes both aspects. Since the four types of transgressions are not filial, and stinginess consists in failing to provide offerings, they are excluded.
[Commentary: Third, regarding filial piety (*xiàoshùn*) in contrast to the extraction of suffering, there are also four permutations:

first, being filial but not extracting suffering, such as the case of Dong Yong and others; second, extracting suffering but not being filial, such as rescuing others from their calamities and distress;
third, being both, which refers to the *Ullambana* Assembly; and fourth, being neither, which refers to those who act with rebellion or minor offenses.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first sentence, Dong Yong was so poor that when his mother passed away, he hired himself out to bury her. He was moved by the grace of a celestial maiden who became his wife to weave silk for him to redeem her from the underworld.
Among these four types of transgressions, there is no filial piety; such a person is a base individual who does not alleviate the suffering of others.
[Commentary] Fourth, regarding filial piety and obedience as a counter-requital for gratitude, there are also four propositions: 1.
Filial piety and obedience that are not requitals for gratitude, such as protecting one’s hair and skin, not being arrogant or reckless, and not speaking what is contrary to the Dharma; 2.

Requitals for gratitude that are not filial piety and obedience, such as assisting with the wheels [of a cart], repaying a single meal, or practicing cultivation to repay a donor; 3. Those that are both, which refers to the *Ullambana* Assembly; 4. Those that are neither.

[The practitioner] proceeds with body and carriage.
