"The Sūtra on the Ullambana Bowl Spoken by the Buddha.
[Commentary] The author states: This sūtra has three translations in total; the first was translated by Dharmanandi during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty. It says:
The *Ullambana Sūtra* was translated during the reign of Emperor Hui (Western Jin) by Dharma Master Faqu; it is also called the *Guānlà Sūtra*.
This is because the text mentions "one hundred flavors of rice," "five kinds of fruit," "water-drawing basins and vessels," "fragrant oil," "incense sticks," and "candles.
Furthermore, the *Jiùběn biélù* (Record of Ancient Editions) notes that another master translated it as the *Bào'ēn Sūtra*, based on the practice to be performed.
Because the name was established [at that time], what is explained here is precisely the first translation. [Commentary:
The "first translation" refers to the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, the fourth sovereign of the Western Jin. The Dharma Master [Kāśyapa]—his full name being Zhu Tanmoluocha;
"Zhu" is his surname, which when translated below means "Dharmarakṣa"—is so called because he translated the scriptures and established their titles.

Next is the translation of the *Guanla jing* (The Sutra on the Bathing and the Full-Moon Festival), translated by Emperor Hui, the son of Emperor Wu and the fifth sovereign. His name is erroneously written as Faju;
it should be Ju (following the *Kaiyuan lu*, it should also be Fahu, though this may be an error within the commentary). It is fully titled *Baninihuan hou guanla jing*.

"Guan" refers to bathing the Buddha, and "la" refers to the completion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Since the sutra explains the methods for making offerings during these two periods after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is named accordingly.

It is said that after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, the four classes of disciples performed the ritual of pouring water and lighting candles on the eighth day of the fourth month and the fifteenth day of the seventh month;

this is what is meant by [the term] "pouring and lighting" (*jìguàn tǐngzhú*). (The *Shū* [Commentary] states that those who interpreted it as "pouring water and lighting candles" lost the collated version of the original scripture.

Furthermore, the *Zànglù* (Catalogue of the Canon) states that ancient records all claimed this was a re-translation and shared the same original text as the *Lán pén jīng* (Ullambana Sūtra), but this is an error. Now, upon examining the text, the wording differs.

If one considers this as a standalone translation, it becomes clear that the present commentary still follows the ancient tradition. (Regarding the term "laxi" [laxi] used by Gushan in his commentary to explain the character *guan* [灌]:

he states that the sixteenth day of the seventh month is the birth of the bhikṣu’s fivefold dharma-body and thus the beginning of the new year; therefore, the fifteenth day of the seventh month is treated as the end of the year. This is not because one only enters the *laxi* period on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, nor because the sixteenth day of the eighth month is the new year and the fifteenth day is the end of the year.

Students should understand this. Regarding the three [catalogues], the "Separate Record" in the old editions is the same as the "Ancient Canon Record" (*Guzanglu*); the *Kaiyuan Lu* states that it is appended [to the main record].

The *Dongjin lu* (Record of the Eastern Jin) is such an example; furthermore, because the translator is lost, it simply refers to "one master. According to the sutra, the full title is the *Bao'en fengpen jing* (Sutra on Repaying Kindness by Offering Bowls).
The preceding passage provides a general enumeration, while the following section specifically identifies [the individuals].

[Commentary] Tripitaka Master Yijing states: "Because [the Buddha] poured forth from his own mouth to gladden the minds of others, and because the teaching accords with their capacities, it is called the 'Buddha’s teaching'.
[Record] "The teaching" corresponds to the phrase "poured forth from his own mouth" above; "accordance with capacities" corresponds to the phrase "gladdened the minds of others" above.
[Commentary]: "Ullambana" is a term from the Western Regions (India), which here means "hanging upside down"; "pen" is a word from the Eastern Land (China), referring to a vessel used for rescue.
According to local customs, it should be called the "Vessel for Saving Those Hanging Upside Down."
[Commentary] "Hanging upside down" describes the nature of extreme suffering. Mencius said:

"In the present age, if a state of ten thousand chariots practices benevolent government, the people will rejoice in it as if being released from hanging upside down. (During Mencius’s time, many states practiced tyrannical policies, causing the people to suffer hardship;

thus, it was like being hung upside down. Now, this phrase is used to translate the [Sanskrit] name. "Pen" is a Chinese word for which no corresponding Sanskrit term has yet been identified. Furthermore—
Relying on the commentary, the remaining details are as explained previously.
[Commentary: This was because the Venerable One’s spirit had sunk into the dark paths; for many days he suffered from hunger and thirst, his life hanging by a thread like one suspended upside down.

Even with the majestic power of the Son of the Buddha, there was nothing that could reach him in his state of extreme suffering. The Buddha then ordered Pūraṇa to provide a hundred flavors of delicacies to serve as a ritual offering.

I pay homage to the Three Honored Ones and look up to the compassionate radiance of the Great Assembly to rescue me from the desperate urgency of being suspended upside down; it is from this very meaning that the title of this scripture is established.

[Commentary] "Carries" (zài) means to bear or, alternatively, to encompass. "Mire and charcoal" (tútàn) is a metaphor for the pressure of suffering, as if one were submerged in mud or placed upon burning coals. Furthermore—
The Book of Documents says: "The House of Xia possessed dark virtue" (referring to King Jie as a ruler who was not enlightened), and "the people fell into mire and fire" (meaning they suffered;

it refers to their distress and exhaustion). [Commentary: As for the term *sūtra* (經), its primary meaning is "thread. It is called a *Kṣudraka-sūtra* (契經); a thread can string together flowers, and a *sūtra* can hold together the warp.
This means that the expressed meaning (*artha*) is like the warp or the flowers, while the expressive text (*vyañjana*) can hold and string them together. Herein, we follow this convention.
In this region (China), the term *jing* (sūtra) is used to designate these texts; borrowing its meaning to assist in naming, the character *qi* (seal/pledge) was further added.

[Commentary] First, based on the translations and exegeses of the Western lands, the local customs of India are considered: just as flowers are strung together with thread and worn upon the crown of the head, a *jing* is like a longitudinal warp capable of holding transverse woof.
Next, following the secular classics of this region (China), the term is interpreted according to the rules of dharma (*fa*).
"Instruction" refers to the constant laws which both the honorable and the humble alike observe; "constant" means that which has not changed from antiquity to the present.
[Commentary] This explains the meaning of "pervasion" among the two meanings of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, as explained above (the remaining four being "fountain," "source," "cord," and "display").
It also explains the meaning of "garland" among the five meanings of the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (the remaining four being "fountain," "source," "cord," and "display").

[Commentary] Regarding the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it encompasses two meanings: "pervading" (*guan*) and "gathering" (*she*). The meaning of "pervading" is the same as here; alternatively, "thread" (*xian*) is equivalent to "pervading," while "sutra" (*jing*) is equivalent to "gathering.

In the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya*, "garland" (*jie-man*) is equivalent to "stringing flowers" (*guan-hua*); the "fountain" (*yong-quan*) takes the sense of being inexhaustible; "origination" (*chu-sheng*) takes the sense of producing goodness;
and "plumb line" (*sheng-mo*) takes the sense of providing a standard for measurement, while "manifestation" (*xian-shi*) takes the sense of clarity.
[Commentary] Next, the explanation of the main text is divided into three parts: first, the introductory section; second, the main body of the teaching; and third, the dissemination section.

The emergence of these three divisions was extensively established by the Great Celestial Master (Dao’an), whose profound judgment perfectly accords with the traditions of the Western Regions, and is followed by all alike throughout past and present.
[Commentary] Regarding the "Initial Division" (Chufen) and the "Three Divisions" (Sanfeng) below, this indicates the original circumstances:
when Xi Zuochi of Xiangyang first visited Master Dao’an of the Eastern Jin, he said, "Xi Zuochi of the Four Seas. Dao’an replied, "The Buddha Dharma fills the heavens; [I am] Shi Dao’an.
From this, people came to call him Miti (Heaven-Filling). Dao’an was the first to classify the scriptures into three divisions. Subsequently...

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that because the three divisions of the "Fruit Portion" (*phala-bhāga*) correspond perfectly with those [three divisions], they are said to be "in profound accord" (*mingfu*).

[Commentary: In the initial "Introduction Portion" (*nidāna-bhāga*), many sūtras possess two types of introductions. First is the "Sequence of Certification and Faith" (*samyak-saṃpratyaya-nidāna*), which refers to the statement:
"Thus have I heard this Dharma from the Buddha. This serves to clearly mark the location where it was preached and to certify that the great assembly heard it together, ensuring there is no error.

The evidence [of the testimony] causes beings to believe and accept the sutra; whether it be extensive or concise, nothing can be attained without faith. For this reason, the beginning of every sutra must include the "Testimony of Faith" (*saddharmapratyayana*).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the time, place, and person are explained, beings will give rise to faith.

Second, the "Introductory Section on the Occasion" (*nidāna*) clarifies the arising of the Dharma that constitutes the main body (*samyak-siddhānta*), such as the jeweled canopy in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* or the light from the brow-hair in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
[Commentary] First, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation. First, the *Sūtra of Testimony* (*Śraddhā-varga*). "Abundant" and "meager" correspond to "extensive" and "concise.
"Stage" (*jiē*) corresponds to "entrance" (*rù*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "Why not speak directly of Prajñā, but instead of dwelling in Rājagṛha?

The answer, as cited in the sub-commentary (*shǔ*), is that "place" refers to the location and "people" refers to the assembly. Within the treatise, three types are briefly indicated; the rest [are explained later].

The third [assembly] is likewise: regarding the arousal of the causes for the purity of the name, five hundred elders offered five hundred precious parasols to the Tathāgata, who joined them into one;
then the Buddha of the Lotus Sūtra emitted light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, and so forth.
[Commentary]: Now, the "Testimony of Faith" (samyag-avavāda) is also called the "General Preface" because it is common to all sūtras;

it is also called the "Postscript" because it did not exist at the time the Buddha preached the Dharma. Furthermore, the "Exhortation" (nidāna) is also called the "Specific Preface" because it varies from sūtra to sūtra;
it is also called the "Preface" because the Buddha himself first initiated the discourse before expounding the "Main Body" (mūla).
[Commentary] The general and specific meanings of the preceding and following titles are understandable.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the first section, the "Certification of Faith":
"Thus have I heard at one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park."
[Commentary] The sub-commentary states: Thus, when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested that the Buddha establish these words.

Regarding the four matters asked, the Buddha answered each one individually: first, he instructed them to dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness (namely: contemplating the body as impure, feelings as suffering, the mind as impermanent, and phenomena as non-self);
second, to take the precepts as one's teacher; third, to silence and exclude monks of evil character; and fourth, [to place this at] the beginning of all sūtras.
All [sūtras] state: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was at a certain place together with a certain assembly of such-and-such persons.
[Commentary]: Regarding the initial text, Ānanda asked four questions: first, he asked upon what basis one cultivates the path; second, he asked who should be taken as teacher;
third, he asked by what means a bhikṣu of evil character should be expelled and disciplined; and fourth, he asked that the beginning of all sūtras should be established [with this formula].
The *Shuyanshu* (Commentary on the *Yanshu*) quotes the Buddha’s response in the *Zhong* (Notes): "By means of four dharmas, one overcomes the four inversions of sentient beings.
Because sentient beings regard the body as pure, suffering as pleasure, the impermanent as permanent, and the non-self as self, these four dharmas are used to overturn them:

first, contemplating the impurity of the body—[the head and other] six parts, the four great elements, and the five faculties, which are provisionally combined and called 'body,' are clearly seen within by means of wisdom."

The five kinds of impurity are: first, the seed; second, birth; third, the dwelling place; fourth, the entire body; and fifth, the ultimate. Second, contemplating that sensation is suffering: the six contacts give rise to the six sensations, and the six sensations give rise to the three sensations—those corresponding to the disagreeable, the agreeable, and the neutral—which produce suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.

Through clear and penetrating wisdom, one realizes that all three sensations are ultimately suffering. Third, contemplating that the mind is impermanent: the six consciousnesses can generate various cognitions through discrimination and grasping; this is called "mind.

Through wisdom, one understands that the mind arises from conditions, does not abide for even a moment, and undergoes arising and ceasing in every instant. Fourth, contemplating that phenomena are without self: [this includes] the two aggregates of perception and formations, as well as the remainder...

Through wisdom, one penetrates all mundane and supramundane phenomena; realizing that all dharmas are without self or what belongs to a self (*anātman* and *anātmīya*), and that they are ultimately unobtainable, one attains the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Within this, the four types of knowledge constitute mindfulness and vision, correctly destroying the inversions;

this is precisely their locus. First, one contemplates the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); third, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*);

and fourth, the two aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), as well as all other dharmas. This is the method for all noble ones and sages, both Great and Small Vehicles.
The Buddha commanded that one should abide by the initial gateway for entering the Path; you should personally apply your mind to this.

[Commentary] Most sutras fully possess the texts of the six kinds of accomplishment, though some may be abbreviated; yet in meaning, they must necessarily include them. These are: first, faith; second, hearing; third, time;
fourth, the teacher; fifth, the place; and sixth, the assembly. If these six conditions are not complete, the teaching will not arise.
Because it must possess six factors, it is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). In the present sutra, the listing of the assembly is omitted.
[Commentary] The first section has two parts. First, the general listing of the six types of common names for accomplishment:
because this single sutra is established by depending upon those six conditions, the following section provides a specific enumeration.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the opening phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), which distinguishes this sūtra from others, each version reflects the intention of the respective translator.
Some say, "Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha," while others say, "I have heard such a Dharma from the side of the Buddha";
both are expressions used to point toward the Dharma.

[Commentary] The first part indicates the differences, referring to the following section where the translator’s intent is expressed; "all below" refers to the harmonization and unification. "Pointing to the Dharma" is a term used to indicate the Dharma, which is the very sūtra being compiled.
[Sub-commentary] Furthermore, regarding "non-self," the intent is to manifest that all sages have realized non-self; as for its presence in other sūtras, it refers to the Āgamas.
It is not difficult to point out that there is no fault in regarding the provisional entity of the five aggregates as being different from the "self" imagined by those with worldly sentiments.

[Commentary] The first part explains the meaning of "there is none now"; the subsequent parts generally address the reasons why other [realms] possess [the self]. Regarding the five aggregates as provisional, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Ordinary persons have three kinds of 'self'—[the views of] seeing, pride, and names; those in training (śaikṣa) have two kinds—[the afflictions of] thought and pride, as their afflictions are not yet exhausted. There is no [self] for those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

[He was] one who had studied [only] the name of "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). Since Ānanda had already realized the state of being beyond training at the time of the First Council, he was merely [possessing] the name;

therefore, the preceding passage states that "all have realized non-self. (Regarding this, Gushan says: "Ānanda was a learner (*śaikṣa*) capable of subduing pride"; my statement that he "realized non-self" is not [in contradiction with this]).
[Commentary] "Hearing" refers to the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) giving rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*) to listen to external sounds.
[Recorded Explanation] Hearing is formed through the conjunction of the three—faculty, object, and consciousness; if one is missing, it is not accomplished. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:

when the ear-faculty is unimpaired (the faculty), sound is within the range of audibility (the object), and one applies the mind with the desire to hear, then hearing occurs (applying the mind is consciousness).
[Commentary: The subsequent phrase "thus" (*evam*) refers to the fulfillment of faith. For "faith" means to say that a matter is thus;
"lack of faith" means to say that a matter is not thus. Therefore, Master Sengzhao said: "It is a term for faithful compliance."

[Commentary] The first part indicates the subject, while the subsequent section explains its characteristics; below, the text cites evidence from Master Zhaogong (Sengzhao), a monk of the Qin dynasty who annotated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* to explain this passage.

[Commentary]: "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the total designation for the completion of the teaching and listening when the teacher and disciples have assembled. It distinguishes this from other times;
that is to say, because there are immeasurable occasions when the Tathāgata preached the sūtras, it is impossible to cite them all individually.

Thus, by using the single word "one," the entirety is briefly encompassed. Furthermore, because the duration of time varies across different regions—being either extended or brief—it is said to be "one."

[Commentary] First, it is generally shown that all sūtra texts—regardless of whether they are extensive or abbreviated—are termed "at one time" (*ekasamaya*) provided they take the beginning and end of the discourse as their ultimate limit;
this excludes other times, meaning times when other sūtras were being taught. Regarding the subsequent specific explanation, there are two parts:
first, an explanation based on the non-uniformity of the teaching of the sūtra; second, an explanation based on the indeterminacy of the region and land. In India (West India), for instance...

There are lands where the year consists of three seasons: twelve months divided such that the sixteenth day of the first month marks the spring equinox, the sixteenth day of the fourth month marks the summer solstice, and the sixteenth day of the eighth month marks the winter solstice.

Alternatively, four seasons may be established by adding the autumn equinox, as in the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, where three months constitute summer and so forth, similar to this land. According to tradition, some establish [the seasons] in this manner.

The six periods (one period being two months): on the sixteenth day of the first month, the season of gradual heat departs; on the sixteenth day of the third month, the season of intense heat departs;
on the sixteenth day of the fifth month, the rainy season departs; on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, the season of lushness departs;

on the sixteenth day of the ninth month, the season of gradual cold departs; and on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month, the season of intense cold departs. Furthermore, one may also stand for a single day at each interval.
The twelve periods (dvādaśa-muhūrta) or eighteen periods may consist of nine periods each for day and night during the two equinoxes;

at the summer solstice, the day is twelve periods and the night is six periods, while at the winter solstice it is the reverse. Alternatively, they may consist of thirty *kṣaṇas* (*muhūrtas*) and so forth; thus, it is said that their duration is indefinite, being either extended or contracted.

[Commentary]: Now, while all the sūtras invariably specify the location rather than the time, some say this is because [specifying the time] would lead to successive difficulties; therefore, it is not employed.

[Commentary] Regarding the citation of the location and the inquiry into the time [of the teaching], the intention of the instruction was to be set forth; however, as the annotations merely presented the interpretations of others without exhausting the underlying principle, it was said that they "invite difficulties.
Since these have now been deleted, it is said they are "not used" (the interpretation by Gu-shan, who forcibly constructed a series of convoluted objections, greatly misses the meaning of the text;
furthermore, as that text is already lost, there is no need to speculate upon it).
[Commentary: Now, examining its intent: as for the location, it refers to the places where he traveled, transformed beings, and resided within the sixteen great kingdoms;

these are finite in number and thus easy to identify. As for the time, it encompasses years, months, seasons, spring, summer, autumn, and winter, as well as days and nights, the twelve double-hours such as *yin* and *mao*, and moments (*muhūrta*).
These temporal transformations are rapid and fleeting; their accumulation is immeasurable, beyond description, and difficult to record.
This is for the purpose of providing a signpost.
[Commentary] First, the fixed locations are indicated: sixteen countries, namely: 1. Aṅga; 2.
Magadha; 3. Kāśi; 4. Kośala; 5. Vṛji; 6. Malla; 7. Ceti; 8. Vatsa; and so forth, as extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Ninilu (9), Pañcāla (10), Aśmaka (11), Vatsa (12), Sura (13), Gandhāra (14), Kamboja (15), and Aparāntaka (16).
While traveling and teaching in these lands, he would reside in monasteries (*ārāma*).
Next, to clarify that the timing was not fixed—referring to the cold and heat, namely winter and summer.
[Commentary]: "Buddha" is the Sanskrit term *buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One. This refers to one who has fully realized the nature and characteristics of both the true and the false.

There are three meanings of "awakening": first, self-awakening to the emptiness of the self (*ātman*), which distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary beings; second, awakening others to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma*), which distinguishes [him] from those of the Two Vehicles;
third, awakening to the fulfillment of the emptiness of both, which accords with original awakening and is called ultimate awakening, or alternatively...
"Great Enlightenment" (*mahābodhi*) and "Sublime Enlightenment" (*vibodhi*) distinguish [the Buddha] from the Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary: The initial translation of the name refers to the following explanation of the meaning. "True" (*satya*) refers to the *nirvāṇa* that is realized; "false" (*mṛṣā*) refers to the delusions and karma that are to be eliminated.

Regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*) and "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): it means to realize the nature as it truly is, and to realize characteristics as being like an illusion. These four characters— [Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*. The bracketed section indicates the reconstructed Sanskrit for the Chinese terms based on standard Buddhist terminology.]

One must explain this by distinguishing between the Great and Small Vehicles; it cannot be applied universally. Ordinary beings are entirely unaware [of the nature], and those of the Two Vehicles are unaware of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Because Bodhisattvas have not yet reached ultimate realization, they are all excluded. Perfect awakening belongs neither to Bodhisattvas nor to those of the Two Vehicles.
The original nature of sentient beings is called "original awakening" (*mūla-bodhi*); that which is attained through awakening from delusion is called "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*).

When the cultivation of the myriad practices reaches its ultimate fulfillment and merges with original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya), it is called "ultimate" (niṣṭhā). In a broad sense, this refers to the Bodhisattvas;
in a subtle sense, it refers to the followers of the three vehicles (triyāna).
[Commentary]: Regarding "at Śrāvastī and so forth," this refers to the accomplishment of the location. The *Tattvārthā-ṭīkā* states that there are two types of dwelling places:

first, the place of the objective field (the range of travel), which is for the sake of transforming those among the laity; second, the place of reliance, which is for the sake of governing the assembly of renunciants.
The former refers to Śrāvastī, and the latter refers to the Jeta Grove. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "By mentioning Śrāvastī, [all such places] are indicated."
[The text] says: "To let those from afar know [that 'the country' is the general term], he mentions Jetavana; to let those nearby know [that 'the garden' is the specific term].
[Commentary]: In the initial passage of Paramārtha’s commentary, he first cites and demonstrates that the "realm" (境界) is the dependent basis (依止) of the land, namely the monastery (寺舍).

By citing the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, he causes those from afar to know [it is Śrāvastī] in order to distinguish it from other countries, and causes those nearby to know [it is Jetavana] in order to distinguish it from other monasteries.

[Commentary: Śrāvastī is here translated as "Hearing Things" (Wénwù), meaning that because it abounds in objects of sensory desire and material wealth, people who possess extensive learning and liberation hear of its fame from afar across various kingdoms.
Tripitaka Master Yìjìng translated the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as "The Great City of Renown."
[Commentary] Regarding the initial translation of the title, "Citing Testimony upon Hearing of Things" means that the excellence of one's own country is described as being praised by other countries.
[Sub-commentary] "The Jeta Grove," etc., refers to the trees donated by Prince Jeta and the site provided by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
He purchased it from Prince Jeta’s garden.

[Commentary: Jeta is translated here as "Victorious in Battle"; he was the crown prince of King Prasenajit, who was given this name because at his birth the king had been victorious in battle against a foreign state.
Anāthapiṇḍada is a title of the minister; his original name was Sudatta.

This is often translated as "Good Giver" (Śrīgupta), meaning he provided for the "giving alone" (the *kṛpaṇa*, who is young and fatherless) and the "giving solitary" (the *ekākī*, who is old and childless);
thus he was called "Good Giver. Furthermore, because he constantly practiced giving, the people of his village praised him and gave him the name "Giver to the Orphans and Solitaries" (Anāthapiṇḍada).

[Commentary] Listing the names, there are two: first, the name of the Crown Prince, Prasenajit, which translates as "Harmonious Joy" (He-yue); second, the name of the Elder, which translates as "Śrīgupta," which is easily understood.
[Sub-commentary] However, the garden was purchased by Sudatta, while the trees were donated by Jeta; thus, the garden is the general term and the trees are the specific. First...
Regarding the combined marking of the garden and the trees: because the rites distinguish between the honorable and the humble, the garden is placed first and the trees second.

[Commentary] From the perspective of the general and the specific, it would be appropriate for the garden to come first and the trees second; however, according to the principle of ruler and subject, the trees should come first and the garden second.
This statement regarding the ritual distinction between the honorable and the humble originates from the *Qu li* (Book of Rites).
[Commentary]: In the Western lands, a monastery is called *saṃghārāma*, which here [in China] is translated as "Garden of the Community" (*zhòngyuán*).

When Buddhism first flowed eastward and reached China, it was housed in the Court of State Ceremonial (*hónglùsì*) to accommodate monks from foreign regions. As the number of monks gradually increased, they were dispersed into separate lodgings;
yet these retained their original designation, all being called "monasteries" (*sì*).
[Commentary] First, he indicates the Western Regions; following this, he indicates the temples of this land. "Temple" (*si*) is the name for an official government office;

the Honglu Si was originally the residence for receiving envoys from the four barbarian regions and distant kingdoms. When Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived, they stayed therein, and thus it took its name.

[Commentary]: Regarding the purchase of the grove and the offering of the trees, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that when the Elder Sudatta went to Rājagṛha to seek a wife for his son, he encountered the Buddha.

The playful dialogue is thus concluded; the subsequent account of the Prince seeing [the tree] and bestowing it upon the two individuals can be understood from the summary at the end.

[Commentary]: Regarding the clan name, there was originally no prefix "Great" (*mahā-*) because those with the same name were numerous; thus, it was added as a distinguishing mark.

[Commentary] The first part indicates Maudgalyāyana’s original cause; the subsequent section clarifies that although the paths of the various sages differ, they are not different insofar as their realization of the cessation [of suffering] is identical.

[Commentary: Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): first, the supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), so called because it realizes and witnesses the basis of supernatural power; it is also termed the "power of mastery over the will" (*kāma-vasitā-vidhi*), for the body reaches wherever one intends to go as soon as one wishes.

Second, the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Third, the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*, literally "heavenly ear"), which means being able to see and hear whether things are near or far, and whether they are forms, sounds, or the like, obstructed by barriers or not.

Fourth, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*)... [is able]... to... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Abhidharma* or *Yogācāra* tradition. The final sentence is incomplete.)*
Because one knows the fundamental events of past lives and former existences, there is the fifth, the supernormal power of knowing others' minds;

this means being able to know all states of mind—whether concentrated or distracted, with outflows or without outflows. Because one knows that the outflows within one's own body have been exhausted, there is the sixth, the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Since these six are all unobstructed, they are collectively termed "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*).
[Commentary] The supernormal power of the realm of miraculous feats (*ṛddhi*) is also called "according to one's will" (*kāmacāra*). This comprises two types:

first, the ability to transform oneself, others, and all worldly phenomena, attaining mastery over them according to one's mind; this is the supernormal power of the realm of miraculous feats, so it is called "attained through wisdom" (*jñānasākṣātkriyā*), as it is realized by generating wisdom within deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Second, the ability to fly swiftly, reaching mountains and obstacles without hindrance; this is "according to one's will."

The divine eye and divine ear refer to the pure derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) produced from the four great elements of the form realm (rūpadhātu), which, having been attained within meditative concentration (samādhi), abide within the sense organs of the eyes and ears;
by means of these, one is able to see and hear the forms and sounds of sentient beings of the six destinies and all the world, whether they are near or far, obscured or unobscured.
As for the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsajñāna), it refers to that which is produced within meditative concentration.

The power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) refers to the wisdom that knows one’s own and others’ past existences—whether one life, two lives, hundreds of thousands of myriads of lives, or even up to eighty thousand great eons—including the events enacted therein (i.e., the *jātaka* tales) and the deeds performed therein (i.e., the *itivṛttaka* tales).

The knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) refers to the wisdom arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that knows the various thoughts, conditions, and mental activities of sentient beings within the six realms of existence, including whether they are in a state of concentration or distraction. Concentration (*samādhi*) is [defined as]...

Regarding the "dispersal and gathering" of the outflows (*āsrava*) and non-outflows (*anāsrava*) of the three realms, as well as the exhaustion of outflows pertaining to both the mundane and supramundane:

this refers to the exhaustion of the outflows within one's own body, wherein, while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one gives rise to untainted true wisdom (*anāsrava-bhūta-jñāna*) to sever and exhaust the fetters of outflow belonging to the three realms.
All six [types of liberation] are attained through the cultivation of sages; the first five are also obtained through karmic retribution.

Life after life, birth after birth, this body is produced and nurtured by one's parents; from the moment it is born until the seventh rebirth, the parents of each successive life serve as the locus of its temporary dwelling.
Since it is only within the mother’s womb that it is conceived, and since she alone provides the milk and embraces it throughout its early life, she is therefore emphasized [as the primary source].

[Commentary] Although those who have not yet taken refuge in the Triple Gem may perform arduous labors, these are not considered of ultimate gravity; therefore, taking refuge in the Buddha is established as the boundary [of such merit].
If one follows the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, which states that all sentient beings have been one's parents, then this extends through many lifetimes back to the beginningless past.
[Commentary] Regarding the gravity of kindness: the parents of this life are the most weighty; others are progressively lighter.

[Record] From previous lives upward, they become increasingly distant; from seven generations to many generations, as they are viewed in successive relation, it is said that the kindness is "progressively lighter."

[Commentary]: Regarding "partial" and "complete" retribution: serving and supporting [one's parents] for one lifetime constitutes the partial; liberating them from many lifetimes constitutes the complete.

[Commentary] Evaluation: Reflecting deeply upon this matter, these words are indeed true. There may be a mother who is not like this, or a child who is not like that;

such cases occur but once in a hundred. This is truly because sentient beings, since beginningless time, have been deluded by ignorance (*avidyā*), clinging to the false while losing sight of the real.
Since their fundamental root is inverted, every branch and detail is likewise so. Alas for the common fools! How can they [understand]?

[Commentary: First, he praises the reality of the matter: that a mother does not love her child, or that a child is rebellious, occurs but once in a hundred cases;

Therefore it is said that ignorance consists in failing to realize that one’s own mind is eternally abiding in quiescence; thus it is called "delusion regarding the truth.
Conversely, one mistakenly identifies the four elements and the six sense-faculties as one's own body and mind, calculating them as "I" and "mine"; thus it is called "clinging to the false.
