[Commentary] The Sub-commentary states: There is a sutra that says, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Maudgalyāyana’s name was Rāhubha and his mother’s name was Citrā.
Rāhubha was about to travel and instructed his mother, saying, "If any guests should come, Mother, you must prepare a meal.
After he had departed, guests arrived, yet the mother did not provide them with food; instead, she again feigned the preparation of a banquet. When her son returned, he asked: "Yesterday..."
When a guest arrived, she asked how she should prepare for them; her mother replied, "Have you not seen the place where food is set out?
Because of the continuous succession of stinginess throughout five hundred lifetimes since that time, it is said that the roots of your transgressions are deeply entangled."

[Commentary] The sequence of the eight sections from beginning to end can be understood. In the first section, because it has not yet been determined from which source [the following] is drawn, it is indicated that there is a sutra (the *Maudgalyāyana Sūtra* currently extant differs from this;
it is a spurious scripture composed by humans). Dīpaṃkara was a Buddha of remote antiquity. No commentary on him has yet been seen.

Now, seeking the meaning through my own judgment: because he is tranquil and yet constantly illuminating, he is called Dīpaṃkara. (The old records state that he is identical to Dīpaṅkara; "Dīpa" and "Dīpan" should be treated as one.)

A lamp with a stand is called a *dìng* (錠); one without a stand is called a *dēng* (鐙). Now, examining the character *dìng*, its primary pronunciation is *dìng* (矴), or alternatively *dìng* (定). It refers to an object made of tin or similar metal. Furthermore, the character *dēng* (鐙) is a vessel for food and is not a lamp.
[Commentary]: "Sin" refers to the karma of body and speech; "root" refers to the mind of stinginess and greed.

Because it continues through many lifetimes and is deeply entrenched and difficult to untie, it is called a "knot. All that arises from stinginess constitutes sinful karma; it is not merely the single instance of false speech at that time.

[Commentary: Body and speech constitute the path of karma; stinginess and greed constitute the path of afflictions; and the continuity [of these] that is difficult to understand constitutes the path of suffering.

To explain the meaning of the profound fetters from the perspective of the lower stages: because one has practiced the karma of stinginess for five hundred lifetimes, it is said that [the afflictions] "arise from stinginess," and so forth.
[Commentary]: This means that stinginess and greed are the roots of suffering, the acts performed are the karma of suffering, and hungry ghosts are the fruit of suffering;
these constitute the three paths. If one follows the ten grave precepts, stinginess is also considered karma, while only greed is considered an affliction (*kleśa*).

[Commentary] First, it shows that the three paths consist of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), which refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and its fruit; it is called a "faculty" (*indriya*) because they arise from birth.
Next, in distinguishing the differences, the ten grave offenses refer to those prohibited by the ten *pārājika* rules of the Bodhisattva precepts.

As for what is stated there—such as "if a disciple of the Buddha is stingy himself or teaches others to be stingy," and so forth—these prohibitions pertain to karma (*karman*) rather than the [affliction of] greed itself, for greed is not explicitly prohibited therein.

Thus, we know that [this karma] belongs to the category of delusion. [Commentary] Question: Are those who have been stingy for five hundred lifetimes humans or ghosts? Answer: They are interspersed as both humans and ghosts; their creation of karma and their experience of retribution mutually support one another.
If they possessed only a human body, it would not be called an evil retribution; if they possessed only a ghostly body, they would not be able to create karma. Or perhaps they are also...
Holding [this view] is not obstructed by principle; however, if the habit of stinginess is not eliminated, it is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*).

[Commentary: The first two lines provide the direct answer. The following four lines mutually clarify [the meaning]: because humans belong to the path of the virtuous, they do not always remain as humans;
because ghosts cannot create karma, they do not always remain as ghosts. Alternatively, the following section indicates the other realms of existence.
The meaning of "departing from the animal realm" includes the hells as well.
[Commentary] Question: Since the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha until the present, the mothers into whom Maudgalyāyana has been born have not been one and the same;
why then does he specifically save that Candraprabhā? Answer: The karmic connection between Candraprabhā and Maudgalyāyana is profound; she was his mother in this life as well.
The mother merely saved this present body; it does not mean she saved that [mother] from a distant age, Qingti.
As for the various other arguments [to the contrary], they all fail to reach the truth.
[Commentary: According to the above scriptural text, the mother of this life is precisely Qingti of a distant age; therefore, one must ask and explain the answer.

The preceding text is intelligible; as for the remainder, which refutes [the view that they are] identical, it should have been explained separately in the ancient commentaries (*gūsu*), but since those texts are lost, we do not know what was said there.
[Commentary: Second, it clarifies that the son’s virtue is meager.
"This is not something that can be remedied by your power alone.

[Commentary] The commentary states: "Your mother’s stinginess was directed toward everything at all times; she has passed through many lifetimes and encountered many people—how could you, as a single individual, have the power to rescue her?"
[Commentary] "Being stingy with all things" means that the objects of one's stinginess are not limited to food alone.
[Sub-commentary] Third, the refutation of the powerlessness of the heterodox:
Although you are filial and your fame moves heaven and earth, the celestial deities, terrestrial spirits, demons, heretics, practitioners of the Way, and the Four Heavenly Kings...
Even the king’s spirits could do nothing against him.
[Commentary] The Subhashita states: The Tripitaka Master said, "Even if you were to invoke celestial spirits from the upper realms and stir earth-deities from the lower regions;
even if you were to capture malevolent demons and ensnare non-Buddhists, unifying the six directions as one family and bringing the eight classes of beings under your total command—"
Even the entire assembly, together with their supernatural powers, could not prevail against him.
[Commentary] "Jidong" (激動) means to stir up; "zongshu" (縱竪) means lengthwise and crosswise. "Lu" (羅) refers to encompassing the four directions, above, and below, constituting the six realms.
As for the "eight classes" (八部), there are two groups of spirits and deities under each of the Four Heavenly Kings; these may include devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth.
This means "to merge.

[Commentary] Regarding "non-Buddhist practitioners (wàidào dàoshì)": this refers to practitioners among the non-Buddhists (wàidào), as distinguished from practitioners within the Buddhist path (nèidào).
This is because when Buddhism was first transmitted to this land, monks were referred to as "practitioners" (dàoshì).
[Commentary]: "Daoist" (daoshi) was originally an honorific title for a son of the Śākya [a Buddhist monk]. Since the Jin and Song dynasties, many people referred to monks as "Daoists";
therefore, translators were particularly required to distinguish this term.
[Commentary]: The Four Heavenly Kings refer to Vaiśravaṇa and others who protect and sustain the world.
[Sub-commentary]: Vaiśravaṇa is the Heavenly King of the North; "and others" refers to Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East, Virūḍhaka of the South, and Virūpākṣa of the West.
[Commentary] Fourth, it clarifies that there is indeed the capacity [to liberate].
One must rely upon the majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Sangha of the ten directions to attain liberation.
[Commentary] The Sub-commentary states: The Tripiṭaka Master says, "A single thread cannot restrain an elephant; one must necessarily rely on many strands. A single person..."
To eliminate karma, one must necessarily rely upon manifold virtues.
[Commentary] The analogy and its corresponding meaning can be understood through comparison.

[Sub-commentary] Now, examining the preceding and following explanations of the text, when the categories of the false and the correct, and the one and the many, are compared, there are four permutations.
First, being correct but not numerous cannot save; this refers to what was previously mentioned regarding you alone. Second, being numerous but not correct also cannot save;
this refers to the aforementioned spirits, deities, malevolent demons, and heterodox paths.

Third, being both numerous and correct can then provide salvation; this refers to the Sangha of the ten directions. Fourth, being neither numerous nor correct, they are naturally incapable [of saving].
Therefore, there is no textual passage in the sutra [to support this].
[Commentary: Regarding the "preceding and following textual passages," the first two phrases constitute the preceding text, while the third phrase belongs to the present section;
viewed in relation to what precedes it, it is the subsequent part. "Ju" (居) means "necessarily."
[Commentary: Fifth, the permission to provide a remedy.
I shall now explain the method of salvation so that all who encounter difficulties may be freed from sorrow and suffering.
[Commentary: The phrase "I shall now explain" is precisely the expression of permission; "the method of salvation" is the matter being permitted.
Regarding the phrase "causing all to be equal": a crossbow capable of holding three thousand *jin* does not fire its trigger solely for a small mouse;
how could the Honored One of the Three Realms unilaterally cause only your mother to be freed from suffering?
[Note] The fifth point, "the matter permitted," refers to the presentation of the True Dharma in the following section. Thirty *jin* constitute one *jun*.
The *Shuowen* states that a "xíshǔ" (mole-rat) is a small mouse. The term "jī" (trigger) refers to the bolt of a crossbow; its application can be understood accordingly.
[Commentary] The sixth section demonstrates the True Dharma, which is divided into two parts: first, the teaching on the method for filial sons to present offerings;
second, the teaching on the ritual for the assembly of monks to receive offerings.
[Commentary] Within the first section, there are further five parts: 1) determining the supreme time; 2) generating the supreme intention;

3) providing the supreme offerings; 4) praising the supreme field; and 5) attaining the supreme benefit. This means that the day of *pravāraṇā* (the invitation for criticism) is the supreme time, like the month of spring’s warmth;
filial piety is the supreme intention, like fresh and excellent seeds; and the hundred flavors and hundred fruits are the supreme offerings.
It is just as when one possesses excellent oxen and uses them for plowing; if one can cultivate the field of the noble and holy ones, it is like fertile soil.
To ensure that parents—whether living or deceased—and their six types of relatives, even up to the seventh generation, leave suffering behind and are reborn in heaven, constitutes a supreme benefit.
Is the purport of the scriptural passage not indeed like this: "A harvest of thousands of sheaves and ten-thousands of bushels, gathered in autumn and stored away in winter"?
However, for the wise, examining this in detail is like pointing to the palm of one's hand.
[Commentary] The five sections at the beginning of the chapter follow a sequential order; "gao-yu" refers to rich, fertile soil, and "xiang" (written as "xiang" here) refers to a carriage box.
"Like pointing to the palm of one's hand" means that it is easy to perceive.
[Commentary] First, regarding the time when the first dhyāna is supreme:
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana that on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, at the time of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) of the Saṃgha of the ten directions.
[Commentary] It is stated: The Sanskrit term *saṃgha* is translated here as "harmonious assembly" (*zhòng héhé*). This means that if there is an assembly but no harmony, it is not [true] *saṃgha*.
A multitude of merchants, officials, and military personnel are not called the Jewel of the Sangha;

nor is a group that is harmonious but not numerous—such as two people of like mind—considered the Jewel of the Sangha. Only when a multitude is harmoniously united does it become a cause for merit and is thus named the Jewel of the Sangha.
[Commentary] Regarding the initial translation, *saṃgha* was first rendered simply as "assembly" (*zhòng*). Later, "harmony" (*héhé*) was added;

this, however, refers to its functional meaning rather than being a direct lexical equivalent. To explain the meaning below: "the group of officials" refers to two public officials whose minds are of one accord.

This is clarified in the *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* regarding the hexagram *Tóng rén* (Harmony with Others), which states: "The way of the noble person is such that they may go forth or remain at home, or remain silent..."

Or it is said: (These words differ from those below in their phrasing, but clarify that the mind is the same. "When two people share the same heart, its sharpness can cut through gold" (this means that when people's hearts are one, their discernment and resolution are as sharp as a blade;

though the nature of gold is hard and rigid, it can be cut—this is a metaphor for extreme sharpness). "Words spoken with a shared heart have a fragrance like orchids" (when the heart is one, the words accord;
they are as fragrant as orchids, meaning they are lovely; "fragrance" refers to the scent of the orchid).
[Commentary]: There are six kinds of harmony: harmony of body, harmony of speech, harmony of silence, harmony of intention, harmony of precepts, and harmony of view;
as well as harmony of benefit and harmony of resources, which mean equal distribution.

[Commentary]: Regarding the six harmonies, the first three are harmony of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-sāmagrī*), while the latter three are harmony of essence (*svabhāva-sāmagrī*). These six are collectively termed "harmony of affairs" (*vastu-sāmagrī*), meaning they are all equal. [Sub-commentary]:
In Confucianism, it is said that the petty man and the superior man may either be in harmony (*he*) or identical (*tong*); now, the Śākya-sons, the bhikṣus, are both in harmony and identical.

[Commentary] The *Analects* states: "The gentleman is harmonious but not conformist (modestly radiant and maintaining correctness); the petty person is conformist but not harmonious (forming cliques for private ends).
If the Buddhist *śramaṇa* is both harmonious and conformist, then the relative superiority or inferiority between him and the Confucian gentleman can be clearly seen.

[Commentary]: The present mention of the "ten directions" indicates that the Dharma is without limitation; how could it be restricted by distinctions between the near and the distant? The term "Saṃgha" is a redundant combination of Chinese and Sanskrit, reflecting the translator’s lack of skill. [Record]:

"The Dharma is without limitation" means it encompasses the entirety of the Buddha's transformation; it refers generally to other dharmas as well, yet here it specifically points to the Saṃgha for the purpose of the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) ceremony.
The fact that these words form a continuous sentence does not necessarily mean they are clumsy; this can be illustrated by the case of the *chánhuì* (repentance). [Commentary:
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) has concluded, and thus the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) may be performed.
There are three days for the *pravāraṇā*: either the fourteenth, the fifteenth, or the sixteenth; here, the middle day is mentioned.

[Commentary] The initial formal explanation of the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat) covers three periods: the "earlier" begins on the sixteenth day of the fourth month; the "later" begins on the sixteenth day of the fifth month;
and the "intermediate" consists of the twenty-nine days in between. The earlier retreat concludes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month;
the later retreat concludes on the fifteenth day of the eighth month; and the intermediate retreat is indefinite according to the specific date. Here, it refers to the seventh [month].
On the fifteenth day of the month, one should immediately enter the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer) retreat.

Three days before the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of invitation), according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, the *Tripiṭaka-uddāna*, and the *Nanshan Shishi Yaoyong Chao*, the *pravāraṇā* must necessarily take place on the sixteenth day. This does not mean that the two preceding days are impermissible;

rather, it is for fear that if one were to leave the boundary before the end of the retreat period, it would constitute a violation of the summer retreat (*varṣa*). The details regarding the summer retreat and the *pravāraṇā* are extensively explained in the Vinaya section.
Since these matters cannot be known without study, I shall not cite them at length.

[Commentary: The character "seng" (僧) here is superfluous and should be removed; furthermore, the omission of a phrase is also a fault of the translation. Why does it not say, "at the time of the communal *pravāraṇā*"?

[Commentary] Regarding the redundant character "Seng" (Saṃgha): the present [author] maintains that this is not the case. The first instance of "Seng" serves as a general heading for the entire teaching, whereas the second instance of "Seng" is restricted to a specific assembly.
The *Shu* (Commentary) points out a translation error, yet its examination of the text is not thorough.
[Commentary]: Regarding "self-indulgence" (*pravāraṇā*): it means that one freely allows others to point out one's own transgressions.

This refers to the fact that even if, during the ninety-day intensive practice of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one does not attain the four fruits [of the path], one may still attain the four dhyānas. Such was the original intent of the Buddha’s establishment of the gates of the teaching;

whether in the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*), or the Sangha, the stages are thus. Although this is the final five-hundred-year period, there are still those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit (merit is...).

[This is] concentration (*samādhi*). Now, as I am about to cross the ocean of suffering, I carefully protect my life-preserving bag (*uḍupa*); yet, fearing that one who stands in the midst of the fray may lose their way, I must rely on the observations of those looking from the sidelines regarding gain and loss.
Even if I have not severed delusions or realized the fruit [of the path], I still hope for the extinction of misdeeds and the arising of merit;
therefore, I bare my shoulder in the midst of the assembly and address the virtuous elders: "May you see my transgressions, hear of my offenses, or suspect me of having committed a fault."

"Please grant me your compassionate words as you see fit; I shall repent accordingly, so that my body and mind will become pure like lapis lazuli—let alone attaining meditative concentration and liberation."
[Commentary] The first part provides a brief indication, which is followed by a detailed explanation in three sections. First, it describes the intent of the Buddha’s teaching;
second, it reveals how the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma were applied to the three periods of time—each lasting one thousand years—and the Final Dharma for five hundred years after that.

This refers to the terminology used in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* clarifies five periods of five hundred years each, of which the first five hundred years is as follows:

The first five hundred years were characterized by firmness in liberation; the second five hundred years, firmness in dhyāna-concentration; the third five hundred years, firmness in maintaining the precepts;
the fourth five hundred years, firmness in extensive learning; and the fifth five hundred years, firmness in contentious strife.

The present reference to the "latter five hundred years" points to this very period, which marks the beginning of the Final Dharma (mofa). Now, he will proceed to explain the three types of self-indulgence (*svairacarya*) that follow.
The merit and benefits are first explained by setting forth the underlying intent: because the three realms are oppressed by suffering without limit or bottom, they are likened to an ocean.
A "floatation bag" refers to a bag made from tanned leather stuffed with bird feathers or blown up with air; using this to cross the sea, one has no anxiety about drowning.

This is a metaphor for the precept-body (*śīla-ātmabhāva*) received by a Bodhisattva, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Therein it says: "Rao... [The text continues with the phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit term].

The *kṣapaṇa* (water-skin): (The *rākṣasa* metaphor illustrates the three poisons and the desire to violate the precepts. First, begging for the whole represents violating the four *pārājika* offenses;

second, begging for half represents violating the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa] offenses; third, begging for one-third represents violating the *sthūlātyaya* offenses; fourth, begging for the measure of a hand represents violating the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* and *pāyattika* offenses;

fifth, begging for the measure of a mote of dust represents violating the *duṣkṛta* offenses (*the sūtra omits the term *pratideśanīya*, which is synonymous with *duṣkṛta*). Thus it is for the Bodhisattva.
This is because they all do not accord with the nature of careful protection and restraint. "In person" (*dangju*) means facing the situation; "as a bystander" (*bangguan*) means observing another.

Therefore, the following clarifies the characteristics of the action: baring one shoulder indicates the presence of an offense. Addressing someone as "Venerable Sir" (*bhadanta*) is a request for testimony from another.
"Seen, heard, or suspected" refers to the basis for raising a transgression. "Transgression," "offense," and "crime" are variations in terminology, as explained below.
This reveals that the training in precepts, concentration, and wisdom benefits individuals according to what each has attained.

[Commentary: Those who make offerings to this [stūpa] can have their efficacy and function known; for does it not rescue and deliver deceased ancestors and provide the conditions for cultivation for those currently living?

Thus, the Tripiṭaka Master said: "On the day monks receive the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and when the great assembly performs the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults), the Saṃgha frequently obtains [merit]."
Because the Way [is realized] through the four fruits of the śramaṇa, one is able to rescue others from distress for seven generations.

[Commentary: The first part correctly demonstrates this; the following section cites scriptural evidence. Because one enters the winter retreat (*varṣā*) and subsequently attains seniority, it is called "receiving the year" (*saṃvatsara*).
[Commentary] Second, generating the superior resolve:
"I shall act for the sake of my parents of seven lifetimes past and those currently undergoing calamities.

[Commentary] The phrase "I shall act for the sake of" refers to the mind capable of rescuing; "for the sake of my parents of seven lifetimes past," etc., refers to the objects to be rescued. This is distinguished according to the objects.
It is called "superior" because it clarifies the mind.
[Commentary] Regarding the clarification of the mind in relation to the object: the object refers to one's parents, as they differ from other people.
[Sub-commentary] As for the "seven generations," the parents who gave birth to one are distinct from the ancestral lineages taken up in Confucianism during times of hardship.

The "intermediate" [category] applies to both the living and the deceased. When one has died, it refers to the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; when one is alive, it refers to illness, pain, shackles, and imprisonment—all of which are termed "calamities.

[Commentary] The previous explanation of the seven generations distinguished this from the Confucian tradition as already shown above; the subsequent explanation of "calamities" applies universally to both the living and the dead.

Regarding "those who have passed away," this refers to those of the seven generations; regarding "those who currently exist," this refers to the present. If one explains this as referring to the physical body born in the present life, then it encompasses both the deceased and the living.

[Commentary]: Although the physical bodies of the seven generations seem somewhat remote, they are all the vessels through which I was born and by which I cultivate the Path. Since I have already received [this benefit]...

How could one ever repay the profound kindness of those who nurtured and raised them? Thus, the Tripitaka Master said: "Since heaven and earth cover and support all beings without wearying of their toil, it is only right that those submerged in the depths of the manifest and the hidden world should respond with infinite gratitude."
[Commentary] The sutra text provisionally mentions seven generations; however, based on the aforementioned period since one first took refuge in the Buddha, it actually encompasses many lifetimes.

"Heaven and earth" refers to one's parents; "tired" (tan) means weary of or loathing [samsara]. "The hidden and the manifest" refers to those who are living and those who have passed away; "sinking into obscurity" refers to being mired in calamities and hardships.
[Commentary: Third, providing superior offerings:

one prepares food of a hundred flavors, the five fruits, water-jars for sprinkling, oil lamps, candles, couches, bedding, and all the sweet delicacies of the world, placing them within the basins to offer to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions.

[Commentary] The statement "possessing food of a hundred flavors" is a general heading. It is like when a person prepares a lavish spread on platters and tables to invite guests, yet says only "eat rice";
thus, "rice" serves as the principal term for the hundred flavors. "Hundred" is a large number and not fixed at exactly one hundred. Regarding the "five fruits":
first, the pitted fruit (*ekāṇḍa-phala*), such as dates, apricots, peaches, plums, and so forth; second, the skinned fruit (*tvaṅ-mukta-phala*), such as...
The three types of *śelu* fruits, such as the *jāmbu*, are tasted by the tongue; the four types of *kapittha* fruits, such as the walnut and pomegranate, are likewise;
the five types of *pañcaphala* fruits, such as the sesame and mung bean, are all tasted by the tongue.
As for the vessels used for drawing and pouring water, such as those for bathing, these are all objects perceived by the body, as are the bedding and mats upon which one lies. As for fragrances...

That which is smelled by the nose, such as oil, incense, and candles used for illumination, as well as that which is seen by the eyes, and even the application of fragrant oils to the body, are all subsumed under the category of the body.
In the Western Regions, all such worldly delicacies are likewise subsumed under the tongue.
Thus far, among the objects of the five desires, only sound has been omitted.

[Commentary] "Initial" refers to the tongue tasting the object of flavor (*rasa*). "Drawing up" refers to the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). "Fragrance" refers to the object of smell (*gandha*). "Oil" refers to the object of form (*rūpa*).

"Upright" means to stand straight; this refers to wax candles. Although the practice of anointing the body with fragrant oil exists in the Western Regions (India), it is not the intended meaning of the sutra and need not be explained here.
The preceding and following sections indicate omissions; nowadays, some may use musical instruments such as conch shells and gongs [in place of these].
In singing and praising [the Buddhas], the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are fully present; yet, when one speaks of the "five desires" (*pañca-kāma*), it seems somewhat inappropriate.

Consider this. [Commentary] Regarding the phrase "exhausting the world," its intended meaning is twofold. "Exhausting" refers to wealth and status: if one possesses wealth and status, one exhausts all that the world has;
if one is poor and lowly, one exhausts the extent of one's own efforts. "Extent" means that one must seek out whatever reaches one's reach; thus, one should understand it in this way.

Whether the offerings be few or many is not fixed; it simply requires the exhaustion of one’s heart. This is likewise like the saying that sacrifices are presented through "conquering sincerity" (*kéchéng*) and are made fragrant by "illustrious virtue" (*míngdé*).
[Commentary] The initial explanation based on the two cases of poverty and wealth immediately demonstrates its essential meaning. The *Shàngshū* says: "The ghosts and spirits have no..."

"Constantly partaking in the sacrifice through the power of sincerity" (meaning that one does not constantly receive the sacrifice, but only those capable of sincere faith do). "The fragrance [arises] from brilliant virtue," as cited previously.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "placed within a basin," this is a scribal error in the translated scripture. How could items such as couches be placed inside a basin? It should rather read: ...
This was written during the Ullambana Offering Assembly.

[Commentary] First, the text presents the following refutation of errors; it should be corrected as follows. Now, examining the Master’s commentary (*shu*), I find he has not fully grasped the intent of the Sūtra.
I shall now provide a structural analysis (*ke*) of the scriptural text: from the beginning up to the "Ullambana bowl," it indicates the items to be offered; at the end...

The second section clarifies the objects of offering; this first part is further divided into two. First, there is a general listing of the four sensory objects (*catvāraḥ viṣayāḥ*) that exhaust all worldly things.

Below, there is a specific mention of the object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*); although it encompasses all things, it specifically refers to the bowl-offering (*pātra-pūjā*). Fearing that it might be treated with negligence or slight, it is singled out for special instruction.
The wise should not harbor partiality or claim this is an error.
[Commentary] The two phrases concerning "making offerings" correctly clarify the practice.
[Recorded Notes] To correctly clarify the practice means that the primary intent in setting out the basins is to make offerings to the Sages; it is to rescue one's kin and uproot their suffering.
By the power of this, the Sūtra states that the Sangha subsumes all three vehicles, as will be detailed below.
[Commentary: According to the original intent of the Sūtra, one need only provide material goods to support the venerable monks who have overcome hardships;
there is no necessity for carvings of gold and jade, the cutting of silks and brocades, or the construction of towering railings and frames. Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master said:
"You must provide the four requisites (vihāra, clothing, food, and medicine) with exquisite materials, and the eight delicacies (rice, flour, salt, vinegar, peaches, pears, plums, and oranges)."
With vegetables such as mustard and ginger, one directs the mind throughout the ten directions and makes offerings with a clarified single mind.

[Commentary] The first part demonstrates the intent of the sutra; the subsequent section rebukes excessive practices. If this was already so in antiquity, it is no cause for wonder that people today are shamelessly presumptuous.
Therefore, the following citation provides proof: the "four things" are a general reference, while the "eight delicacies" are a specific designation.
[Commentary] Fourth, praising the supreme field of merit: on this day, all the holy assembly—
some were in mountain retreats practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), some had attained the fruits of the four paths,

some were walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*) beneath trees, some possessed the mastery of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) while teaching and transforming *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and some were [Bodhisattvas of] the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)...
The Great Being, manifesting as a bhikṣu through his skillful means, was amidst the great assembly; all were of one mind as they received the *pātra-bhara* meal.
Possessing the path of the noble assembly and pure precepts, his virtue was vast and boundless.

[Commentary] The sub-commentary states: The first two phrases praise the time in reference to the person and provide a general heading; the final two phrases praise the person by way of their majestic deportment and serve as a concluding summary.
[Record] Since the Sūtra designates this specific day, it says "praising the time"; what follows later, "his virtue is vast and expansive," refers precisely to this.
In the section on "Dignified Conduct" (*īryāpatha*), the characters are omitted below.

[Commentary]: Among the intermediate categories of persons and dharmas, there are five pairs, though the text is not in sequential order. These are: first, the pair of dwelling in mountain retreats or under trees versus realizing the four fruits and the six supernormal powers;

second, the pair of practice for one's own benefit versus benefiting others (the practice of walking meditation is for self-benefit, while teaching and transforming others is for the benefit of others).

Regarding the training in benefiting others, there are the pairings of precepts and meditative concentration (each having its own textual basis), as well as the pairing of persons into great and small,

which is also termed the pairing of the provisional and the real (wherein *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* are the real and the small, while *bodhisattvas* of the ten stages are the provisional and the great).
[Commentary] The initial general indication refers to what follows below, where the self and others are distinguished;

by comparison with this, one should understand that while the followers of the Two Vehicles are not incapable of transforming others, they do not possess the profound and vast vows of a Bodhisattva, which is why other texts speak only of their "self-benefit.

Regarding the contrast between precepts and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there are respective textual passages for each: the former mentions "meditative concentration in the mountain valleys," while the latter states "possessing purity."

Regarding the commentary on the "Medium" version of the *Śīla-sūtra* which contrasts the Great and Small Vehicles, it identifies the Two Vehicles as "real," meaning they are practitioners of actual practice rather than provisional manifestations.

According to this treatise, the acceptance of offerings must apply universally to the sages and ordinary beings of both the Great and Small Vehicles; while the sutra mentions the Three Vehicles, it does so from the perspective of the most eminent.
[Commentary: Furthermore, summarizing these, they do not exceed the categories of person and dharma, corresponding to the three trainings and the three vehicles.

From the beginning up to the fourth fruit [of the śrāvaka path] refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Next, from "or below" up to "teaching and transforming with mastery" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).

All of these correspond to the three phrases below, which refer to pure ethical discipline (*śīla*). As for the "three vehicles," they are the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the great beings of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

[Commentary] Regarding "persons and dharmas": "dharmas" refers to the three trainings, and "persons" refers to the three vehicles. As for the "ten stages," the first is the Joyous (also named Entering the Treasure Place);

the second is the Stainless; the third is the Luminous (also named Radiant Wisdom); the fourth is the Blazing (also named Flame-Wisdom); the fifth is the Difficult to Conquer; the sixth is the Manifest...

The first seven are the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), the eighth is the Acalā (Immovable), the ninth is the Sādhumatī (Excellent Wisdom), and the tenth is the Dharmameghā (Dharma-Cloud) (as derived from the Tiantai *Jieshu*).

Now, examining these divisions in detail, the sequence is disordered and the textual structure is difficult to comprehend; therefore, I shall provide a further topical outline (*kejie*) and explanation. This is divided into three parts: first, the two initial lines provide a general heading;
alternatively, they may be placed below as a specific enumeration, which is identical to the following general conclusion. Within the specific enumeration, there are further two sections.

At the beginning, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas constitute the Saṃgha of the Two Vehicles; alternatively, from the ten stages (bhūmis) down to those within the great assembly, they constitute the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
Within the context of the Two Vehicles, there are again two [aspects]: the first four phrases praise their virtues, while the final phrase points to the individuals.

Furthermore, among these four phrases, the upper three concern one's own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*), and the lower phrase concerns the transformation of others (*parārtha*). Within the section on one's own practice:

Dhyāna-samādhi can be understood as attaining the fruits and severing delusions, which pertains to the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*); walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) for the purpose of regulating the body pertains to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, dhyāna-samādhi and walking meditation must rely upon a specific location; however, the attainment of the Way and the transformation of others are not restricted to a particular place.
The first two lines of the verse clarify the acceptance of offerings, while the latter three lines praise his virtue and conduct: the first line praises his practice, and the [following] two...
The phrase "the depth and breadth of what has been realized" describes the vastness and profundity of the realization; only by analyzing the text in this way can one perceive the intent of the sutra.

Mount Gushan states that the provisional manifestation of the Ten Stages is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, wherein one secretly maintains the practice of a bodhisattva while outwardly appearing as a śrāvaka.
He further poses a challenge: "How does this sutra differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? He answers: "This [sutra] merely speaks cryptically of the provisional."
Although the person is not explicitly named in the present passage, it clearly states that they are a "provisional manifestation" (*upāya-nirmāṇa*);
how, then, can this be considered secret? Let those who possess discernment attempt to evaluate this.

[Commentary: "All with one mind" refers to the harmony of intention; it means that at the time of receiving offerings, all equally exercise a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*), a profound and earnest mind, a mind of compassion, and a mind of gratitude for the causes [of their past] and a heart of salvation.
Although people differ in rank—whether ordinary or sage—and in virtue—whether superior or inferior—the mind they exercise is one and no different; therefore, it is called "the same."

[Commentary] According to the intent of the Vinaya, "harmony" (*sāmagrī*) refers specifically to the acceptance [of a formal act] (*kṣānti*) in relation to legal matters (*dharmakriyā*). For the time being, this term is taken in its general sense of "conformity.
"Shame" (*hrī*) and "modesty" (*apatrāpya*) pertain to one's own benefit, while "compassion" (*karuṇā*) and so forth pertain to the benefit of others.
[Commentary]: "Receiving *pātra-bhara* rice" refers to the rice within the bowl. In Sanskrit it is called *pātra*, which is translated here as "vessel" (*yingqi*).
The character "he" (和) is an error. In current usage, it is simply called "bowl" (*bo*), which is an abbreviation.

[Commentary]: Regarding *pātravāra*, it is interpreted as "receptacle for alms. If one follows Master Ying’s *Jīngyìnyì* (Explanations of the Phonetics and Meanings of the Sūtras), which states that *pātravāra* is translated here as "food at will" (*zìzìshí*), this seems more consistent with the meaning of the text.
[Commentary]: The title of the sutra uses the character "pen" (basin), which is equivalent to "po" (bowl). At the time of translation, it was titled "pen" in accordance with local custom;
both "pen" and "po" refer to vessels. The Tripiṭaka Master explained the title as "the vessel for salvation."
[Commentary] Regarding the citation of the Tripiṭaka below, that [text] explains the title as "The Vessel for Rescuing Those Hanging Upside Down.
[Sub-commentary] This single phrase of the sūtra precisely clarifies that the virtuous monks (bhadanta) receive the offerings of the Ullambana bowl during the ceremony of self-indulgence (pravāraṇā).
[Commentary] Because the noble assembly receiving the meal is itself the establishment of the alms-bowl.
[Sub-commentary] Fifth, obtaining superior benefits:
those who make offerings to such self-indulgent monks will, in their present life, enable their parents, six types of relatives, and kinsmen to attain liberation.

The sufferings of the three evil realms shall be liberated at that very moment; clothing and food will appear spontaneously. If one's parents are still living, they shall enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years;
if the parents of seven generations have been reborn in heaven, they shall attain sovereign mastery, being born by transformation amidst the radiant flowers of the celestial realm.

[Commentary] The commentary states: This single recitation of the scripture contains two sections of meaning. The first half refers to those who, through the power of the compassionate vow, are freed from suffering;

the latter half refers to those who, through the power of the benevolent vow, attain happiness. Within this happiness, there is a distinction between those who remain [in this world] and those who have passed away.
[Commentary] The initial statement, "these monks who perform the *pravāraṇā*," refers to what was previously explained regarding the five pairs.
[Record] The first passage indicates that the aforementioned five pairs do not exceed the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
[Commentary]: "Parents of the present life" refers to the parents who gave birth to this very body;
it does not mean that those who have not yet passed away are designated as "present. Therefore, the benefit is specified as "exiting the three miserable realms.

As for the phrase "parents currently not yet deceased," there is a passage further below stating, "May they enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years. One should not cite this again, as the Tripiṭaka Master has misunderstood it.
To provide a *vyadhikaraṇa* (separate-subject) analysis here is utterly contrary to the meaning of the text.

[Commentary] In the first part of the following section, the current interpretation is presented; "it is not the case that... below serves to exclude confusion with the Tripiṭaka, while the subsequent passage criticizes erroneous interpretations.

A questioner asks: For what reason can the present [state] bring one out of the three miserable realms? The answer is: it is by verifying the fruit through its cause; this is what is meant by "difference" (*viśeṣa*).
This is the explanation.

[Commentary: The "six relations" (*ṣaṭ-kaula*) refer to parents, brothers, and spouses (some say "male and female," excluding brothers). "Relatives" (*jñāti*) refers to all kinsmen by marriage, encompassing both those on one's father's side and those on one's mother's side.
[Commentary] The "six relatives" are derived from the commentary on the *Laozi*. Within that commentary, it is sometimes said that the source text is unknown;
however, according to the commentary on the *Hanshu*, the six relatives consist of parents, brothers, wife, and children.

These differ depending on who establishes the definition, yet all kinsmen by marriage are also included as "relatives. "Outside" refers to the maternal clan, while "inside" refers to the paternal clan.

[Commentary: "Emerging from the three miserable realms and attaining liberation" generally clarifies the departure from suffering. As for "food and clothing being provided spontaneously," this refers to being reborn in the human realm after having turned away from the three miserable realms;
thus, it belongs to the section on "extracting from suffering. It may also be understood as immediately obtaining happiness, which would belong to the subsequent section.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage on "food and clothing appearing naturally," there are two interpretations. The former meaning is correct; the latter interpretation follows the literal text while also incorporating the subsequent doctrinal sense. [Sub-commentary]: From the phrase "If the parents...
onwards, it clarifies that they obtain happiness regardless of whether they are living or deceased; the textual structure is clear. As for "heavenly flowers and light," it refers to the heavens...
"The light of exquisite flowers" is a brief indication of the characteristics of bliss.

[Commentary] "Exquisite flower-light" refers to the adornments of the supporting environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the upper realms; as it is not limited to these two alone, it is said to be a "brief indication."
[Commentary] This concludes the second section above: the ritual for the Sangha receiving offerings.

At that time, the Buddha commanded the Sangha of the ten directions to first perform a *svastyayana* (blessing) for the donor’s family, wishing that their parents of seven generations might practice the mind of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and only then receive the food. When first receiving the food, it was first placed before the Buddha within the stupa or monastery.
After the assembly of monks had finished offering prayers before the Buddha, they proceeded to receive the food themselves.
[Commentary] The commentary states: In this passage, the first half purifies the three karmas, while the second half fulfills the three jewels.
[Commentary] From the beginning up to "then receive the food" constitutes the first half; from "having first received" onwards is the second half.

Although the meaning of the text according to this division is not yet explicit, upon careful examination, it can be seen that the first half instructs on the mental application (*manasikāra*), while the second half correctly teaches the ritual for receiving [the food].
This may be verified by looking into the text.

[Commentary: In the preceding section, the recitation of mantras constitutes the verbal karma (*vākkarman*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) constitutes the mental karma (*manaskarman*), and receiving food constitutes the bodily karma (*kāyakarman*).
[Commentary: In the subsequent section, the stupa represents the Buddha; the recitation of mantras represents the Dharma; and receiving food represents the Saṃgha.
To receive from another and then eat is the legal rule (*vinaya*); thus, the word "receiving" (*pratigraha*) also pertains to the Dharma.

[Commentary] The Vinaya regulations stipulate that whenever a bhikṣu eats, he must receive the food from a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant); to handle it himself without receiving it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Therefore, it is said that the legal codes are thus. The Sūtra says, "First place [the food] before the Buddha," which refers to a secular residence;
"before the stūpa or temple" refers to a monastery (*saṃghārāma*). (Gushan [Zhiyuan] distinguishes this based on whether the Buddha was in the world or had entered parinirvāṇa.)
[Commentary]: "Stūpa" is a corruption of the language of the borderlands; the correct term is *stūpa*, which means a "lofty and prominent place.
Here, the meaning applies generally to both halls and stupas; a stupa enshrines śarīra (relics), while a hall enshrines Buddha images.
[Commentary] To say "stūpa" (塔婆) and then abbreviate it to "tā" (塔) is both erroneous and overly concise. The following section demonstrates the general meaning.
[Sub-commentary] From here on is the seventh major section of the text: The Filial Son’s Realization.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the assembly of great bodhisattvas were all filled with great joy; Maudgalyāyana’s weeping and sobbing ceased entirely.
[Commentary] The subcommentary states:
Since pure karma has been perfected, one must know that suffering has been transcended. By observing the cause, the result is verified; the resonance of the sound does not err.
Therefore, he stops crying out of joy. It is like being in the world’s prisons and entrusting oneself to a person of great power;
once the bribe has been paid, his mind is already joyful.

[Commentary] "Having already accomplished" means that because one has received the teachings from the Buddha, one will certainly have no doubts regarding what is practiced hereafter; thus, one contemplates the cause.
The verification of the fruit corresponds to the two lines [of the verse]; the sound responding without error is a metaphor for the aforementioned cause and effect.

This means that just as a voice answering an echo is invariably correspondent, the sutra says "xièrán" (釋然), which means to dissipate or disperse. Below, worldly affairs are cited to clarify the intent of the sutra;
"huì" (賄) is pronounced with the *hū* and *zuì* finals, and it also refers to wealth.
[Commentary: Eighth, the mother receives benefit.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana’s mother was immediately liberated from the suffering of a hungry ghost for one kalpa on that very day.

[Commentary: The narrative states: Maudgalyāyana heard the sutra and received the instruction; however, the establishment of the offering of bowls (pén-gòng) should properly take place at another time.
The statement that "one is now freed from the realm of hungry ghosts" at this point in the sequence of the sutra is a deficiency in the translation;
it should have been recorded at the conclusion of the main body of the text by the compilers, who stated:

"At that time, having heard this Dharma, Maudgalyāyana reached the fifteenth day of the seventh month, prepared the *pén-gòng* (vessel offerings) for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and once the monks had completed their self-examination, his mother was immediately liberated on that very day."
The suffering of hungry ghosts for one kalpa is thus clear both in its literal meaning and its underlying significance.

[Commentary] The initial section describes the deficiency in response; the following section supplements it with the subsequent meaning. It may be that when the sutra was being preached, it coincided exactly with the end of the summer retreat, and preparations were made immediately;
hence the phrase "at this time," etc. Furthermore, within the preceding demonstration of the Right Dharma, five sections were provided to detail the offerings of the ritual basin.
According to the Dharma, it is sufficient to simply state "at this time" or "on this day," as the meaning already encompasses the performance of offerings; thus, there is no deficiency.
[Commentary] Therefore, the Tripitaka Master said: "Once the filial son has presented his offerings at this hour, the compassionate mother shall have her calamities removed on this very day.
How great indeed is the power of the Sage—how swift it is!"
[Commentary] As for the duration of years and kalpas during which the hungry ghosts undergo suffering, it remains to be examined and recorded.

[Sub-commentary] One cycle of increase and decrease of the physical world constitutes one *kalpa*. Although Maudgalyāyana’s deceased mother was destined to fall into the realm of hungry ghosts for one such *kalpa*, the relationship between the years and months of that realm and those of the human world, as well as the specific length of that *kalpa*, have not yet been found in the source texts; hence it is said, "it remains to be examined."
[Commentary] From here below is the third major section, the *Pravāraṇa* (Circulation) portion. Within this text there are three parts.
[Record] This means that because this teaching reaches infinitely, it is like the flow of a river that never becomes obstructed; therefore, it is called "circulation" (*pravāraṇa*).
[Commentary]: First, the formal request.

Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Because my biological mother has been able to receive the power of the merit of the Triple Gem and the majestic spiritual power of the Sangha, all disciples of the Buddhas in future ages should likewise offer the *bowl-liberation* (*ulambana*)."
"Is it permissible to perform the *bō* (alms-bowl) rite of salvation for one's present parents, and even for parents up to seven generations back?
[The Commentary] states: Examining these words, they likewise refer to the period following the offering of alms, rather than being the events of a single occasion;
it was only at the Piṇḍola Cave that they were finally compiled together into a sutra.
[Commentary]: Since the request was made again after the basins had already been set out, this was not a single occasion; many sūtras are like this.
The Piṇḍola Cave is where Ānanda held the council, located at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
[Commentary: Maudgalyāyana loved his own kin and extended that love to others, just as Ying Kaoshu admonished Duke Zhuang, saying...
[Recorded Explanation: The following citation of Kaoshu serves as an analogy for Maudgalyāyana. Regarding the note "...and so forth," the *Zuo Zhuan* states:
"Duke Wu of Zheng married a lady from Shen, known as Wu Jiang (Shen was the name of a state). She gave birth to Duke Zhuang and Gong Shu Duàn (Gong is pronounced *gōng*). Duke Zhuang..."

Born while his mother was awake, he startled Lady Jiang, who consequently came to detest him. She loved Gong Shu Duan and wished to establish him [as the Crown Prince], repeatedly petitioning Duke Wu for this;
however, the Duke did not grant her request. When Duke Zhuang ascended the throne, Lady Jiang and Shu Duan conspired to usurp the state.
Upon hearing that the troops were attacking them, Shu Duan fled to Gong (the state of Gong, after which he was styled Gong Shu Duan), whereupon [Duke Zhuang] subsequently placed him in confinement.

The Lady Jiang placed [her son] at Chengying (Chengying is a location in Zheng; "zhì" is pronounced as "zhì," meaning to place) and swore an oath to him, saying, "Until we reach the Yellow Springs, we shall not see one another again" (the springs beneath the earth are thus called the Yellow Springs).
Subsequently, she regretted this. Kaoshu was the border-guard of Yingguo (the official in charge of the frontier boundaries);
having heard of the matter, he presented an offering to the Duke. The Duke granted him a meal, but he set aside the meat while eating. The Duke asked him about this, and he replied:
"The commoners all have mothers who have tasted the food of the commoners, yet none have ever tasted the soup of Your Majesty; I beg to take this and present it to them.
The Duke said, "You have a mother to whom you can present it, but alas, I alone have none. Kao Shu asked, "May I ask what you mean by this?
The Duke told him the circumstances and confessed his regret. He replied, "What cause for concern does Your Majesty have? If—"
They dug through the ground down to the springs so that they might see one another; who would say this was not so? (The term "tùì" refers to the underground passage used today for burial.

The Duke followed her advice. Upon entering, he recited a poem: "Within the great tunnel, its joy is harmonious and melting. (This is a poetic recitation; "róng-róng" describes a state of harmonious happiness.

Lady Jiang, having gone out, recited: "Outside the great tunnel, its joy is relaxed and flowing. ("xiè-xiè" describes a state of ease and dispersal; "xiè" is pronounced like "yè. Thus, she became his mother once again.
The son was as he was at first. The Gentleman said: "Ying Kaoshu was purely filial; his love for his mother extended even to Duke Zhuang.
(Pure means sincere and earnest; *shi* is pronounced *yi*). Thus, Kaoshu’s influence reached only one person, whereas the Honored One’s grace is widely bestowed upon all beings.
One should know that the Great Being manifested as a Śrāvaka as a skillful means to deliver sentient beings; therefore, he acted as the initiator [of this narrative], which remains so unto this day.

[The text] states: "All have received its bounty. This citation of past precedents is intended to clarify the text and minutely examine the execution of the work; yet, in truth, they are not of equal rank.
[Commentary: Second, the praise and request.
The Buddha said: "Excellent! You have asked well. I was just about to speak, and you have asked again. [Commentary] The author states:
The first phrase praises [the questioner], calling it "excellent" and "well-asked," because it deeply accords with the Sage’s mind. The latter two phrases explain the reason for this:
"just about to speak" refers to the occasion of the inquiry; as the capacity of the questioner and the response of the Buddha meet, there is a subtle penetration and a hidden resonance.

"Kuai" (excellent) means that the principle is appropriate. [Commentary] "Great goodness" refers to the fact that the principle is fitting; "appropriate questioning" refers to its being suited to one's own mind; "latent penetration" refers to the faculty (*nengquan*) meeting the Buddha;
and "secret response" refers to the resonance (*ganfu*) responding to that faculty. Because they harmonize spontaneously without prior deliberation, it is called "latent and secret."
[Commentary: The Buddha’s original intention was to teach that filial piety is the greatest virtue; because the matter of uprooting suffering is weighty; because the *Ullambana* rite is supreme;
and because the assembly beheld the Venerable One, whose superior conditions had matured and who was ready for conversion.
[Commentary] These four meanings seek the Buddha’s intent and summarize the ultimate destination: there is nothing that does not benefit sentient beings through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

How could they be limited to a mere number of points? His compassionate salvation extends beyond a single class of beings. Filial piety is the greatest because it is the root of the Way and its Virtue (*moralitās*);

the extraction from suffering is paramount because it is the practice of a Great Being (*mahāsattva*); and the *Ullambana* Dharma is supreme because it is both the objective realm and the subjective mind.
Because they differ, and because those who perceive the superior conditions will see the verification swiftly.
[Commentary] Third, the response to the request consists of five parts.
[Commentary] First, the arising of the teaching and its practice.
Good son, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, kings, crown princes, ministers, grand secretaries, high officials, the three dukes, the myriad officials,
or commoners who practice loving-kindness and filial piety, they should all first, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month—
the day the Buddha rejoices and the Sangha performs the *pravāraṇā*— on behalf of their present living parents and their deceased parents of seven generations, [perform offerings].
One should place food of a hundred flavors within the *urunda-bhājana* (alms bowl) and offer it to the monks of the ten directions who are observing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

[Commentary] The author states: Although there are distinctions between the noble and the lowly, and differences between the monastic and the lay, as well as between those of the Way and the secular—save for those born by transformation or moisture—all beings without exception have fathers and mothers.
Even affectionate birds and parrots understand how to contemplate their debt of gratitude; how much more so should this be true for human relations?
The benefits and harms of filial piety have already been set forth in the preceding discourse; once one has recognized right from wrong, one must rely upon the correct path.
Therefore, it is said that "one should first [act] for the sake of those who gave birth to one," and so forth.
[Commentary] "Noble" refers to kings and ministers; "lowly" refers to the myriad commoners; "monks" refers specifically to the ordained clergy, both male and female.

In common parlance, this term generally encompasses all classes, from the noble to the lowly, across the six realms of existence, which do not exceed the four modes of birth—namely, viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born.

Regarding the two modes of viviparous and oviparous birth, they invariably involve parents. As for the "filial bird" (*ciāo niǎo*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the "filial bird" because it is able to regurgitate food to nourish its mother.
As for the "parrot" (*yīngwǔ*), the *Zá bǎozàng jīng* relates that in a past life, the Buddha was at the Snow Mountains.
In a former life, he was a parrot whose parents were both blind; he constantly gathered flowers, fruits, and rice stalks to provide for them.
Those blind parents were none other than Śuddhodana and Māyā. However, while the story of the compassionate bird is a manifestation of the present, the parrot of the past was a different being.
Thus, the distinction between their identities is clearly revealed by the presence of these differing benefits and interests.

Within the way of filial piety, both transgressions and blessings are present; because this is explained before entering the formal chapters of the scripture’s meaning, it is called a "prefatory discourse" (*xuántán*), where *xuán* means "prior.

The scripture states that the "Three Ducal Ministers" refers to the positions of Grand Preceptor (*dàshī*), Grand Tutor (*tàifù*), and Grand Guardian (*tàibǎo*) established in the Zhou official system.

[Commentary]: According to the established regulations, whether one necessarily performs or does not perform [an act] constitutes a violation of those regulations; therefore, this also pertains to the formal teachings (vinaya).
For this reason, the preceding section also belongs to the Vinaya Piṭaka. [Record]: The Sūtra says:

"In all cases, that which is non-regulation (a-śikṣāpada), whether performed or not performed, is without offense and further does not constitute a violation of the regulations. This refers to the preceding text.
Based on this, it is further clarified that what was previously indicated as "not being permissible to accept" is indeed not so.
[Commentary: Although the Buddha is without [worldly] sorrow or joy, his manifestation of joy on this day is for the sake of responding to specific conditions.
The reason the Buddha originally appeared in the world was solely to exhort people to practice; thus, when he sees people creating karma, he feels compassion, and when he sees people...
To cultivate the path is indeed a joy. Now that the ninety-day preparatory period for the bhikṣus has concluded, their sincerity is redoubled;

throughout the trichiliocosm, all are likewise so. This accords with the Buddha’s original intent—how could one not rejoice on this day? To set out a basin of offerings on such a day brings immense merit.
[Commentary] That the Buddha has neither sorrow nor joy refers to his own practice; that he manifests joy refers to his transformation of others.
The "trichiliocosm" refers to a single sphere of transformation.
[Sub-commentary] Second, the teaching on making vows.
May my present parents live for a hundred years, free from illness and all afflictions of suffering;
may their ancestors for seven generations be freed from the misery of the hungry ghosts and be reborn among humans and devas, where their merit and happiness shall be boundless.
[Commentary] The exposition states: That which is cultivated must rely upon the gate of practice, and that which is attained must arise from the power of aspiration.

Aspiration is the mind’s longing; through it, one seeks to ensure the peace of both the living and the deceased. For the living, it means preserving life within the human realm, remaining forever free from illness and affliction.

For the deceased, it means transferring the spirit to the heavens, forever severing the path to the dark underworld. When practice and aspiration support one another, there is nothing that is not beneficial.

[Commentary] In the scriptural text, the two characters "wishes that" (*yuàn shǐ*) constitute the agent of the wish (*néng yuàn*), while "the seven generations [of ancestors], etc. constitutes the object of the wish (*suǒ yuàn*).

The first explanation concerns the agent of the wish: the preceding phrase may be linked to the previous section, and the subsequent phrase corresponds to the word "joy" (*lè*) in this chapter, which should be read with a departing tone (*qù hū*).
"Surviving" refers to the present life; "perished" refers to the seven generations. Each of these may be correlated with the scriptural text as follows.

The final two lines summarize that there is nothing not beneficial; this means that one will surely obtain results. A person who possesses both eyes and feet will certainly reach their destination, whereas in worldly affairs, even with aspirations and actions, success is not necessarily guaranteed. Therefore, [this practice] is superior.
[Commentary]: This practice is performed regularly by the Three Teachings.
Disciples of the Buddha who cultivate filial piety and obedience should constantly, in every thought-moment, remember their parents, even up to their parents for seven generations.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year, they should always use filiality and compassion to remember the parents who gave them birth and perform this rite on their behalf.
One offers the *Ullambana* bowl to the Buddhas and the Sangha to repay the kindness of one’s parents who nurtured and loved one with compassion.

[Commentary] The Subcommentary states: This clarifies that those who are disciples of the Buddha and practice filial piety should perform this; conversely, it shows that those who are not disciples of the Buddha and are unfilial may, at their discretion, omit the offering of the bowl.
To "constantly remember" from moment to moment means without beginning or end. "Nurturing" refers to long-term upbringing.
Because this matter consists of the affection of the heart, one should first initiate practice and resolve to repay it. The rest of the text is easily understood.

The Tripitaka Master said: "Since the parents' bonds of love do not leave the mind for even a single thought-moment, a filial child repaying their kindness must provide offerings without ceasing year after year."
[Commentary] First, regarding the persons taught—the disciples of the Buddha—they are so called because they receive the Teacher’s instruction.

Regarding those who cultivate filial piety and obedience, they do so because they recognize the gravity of their debt of gratitude. "Moment by moment" and so forth follows. Next, regarding the dharma taught:

since parents nourish and love us with compassion that has no beginning or end, a filial child must initiate practice and make vows; thus, one must repay them through action throughout one's entire life and through vows.
The passage stating that "the mind cannot be lacking even one [factor] when facing the Dharma" can be understood by referring to the supporting evidence cited in the subsequent text.
[Commentary: Fourth, the exhortation to receive and uphold:
If all disciples of the Buddha, they should reverently uphold this Dharma.
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By the power of faith one receives [the teaching], and by the power of mindfulness one maintains it.
What is here termed "receiving" (*fèng*) carries the same meaning as "receiving," and "all should" exhorts one to apply these two powers.
[Commentary] Without faith one cannot receive [the teaching], and without mindfulness one cannot maintain it; "exhortation" (kshu) refers to admonition.
[Sub-commentary] Five: Rejoicing and Following the Command.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the disciples of the four assemblies rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

[Commentary] The sub-commentary states: Regarding the "four classes," they refer to monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; alternatively, some say they include humans, devas, nāgas, and ghosts. Because there is doubt [regarding the latter], both versions are preserved.
[Record] As for the phrase "both are preserved," it is because each has its own scriptural source.
[Commentary: Since all living beings rely upon and depend on their parents, parental kindness is equal to that of Heaven and Earth.

Although one may be supremely filial, if one does not find the proper way, [the debt remains]. Now, having received this divine method and witnessed its miraculous efficacy, I am certain it can eliminate the calamities of seven generations and repay the arduous labors of my two parents. Knowing in my heart where my purpose lies, I am therefore filled with joy.
"I joyfully accept your command.

[Commentary] The initial statement regarding the depth of his grace refers to the fact that he brought all living beings into existence. Since the term "living beings" (shēnglíng) is a general designation applicable to all, it here specifically refers to the fourfold assembly who rely upon him as their parents.
This is consistent with the verse cited previously: "Without a father, on whom can one rely? Without a mother, what can one depend upon? Following this, next...
In the first two lines of the opening section of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the various capacities of sentient beings are described as being without a [fixed] dharma;

this single character "this" (此) refers to those living beings who have not yet attained the gate. If it were not for the Buddha’s teaching, no one else would know [this]. Below, the text clarifies the joy of attaining the Dharma;
"spirit" (*shen*) refers to the marvelous, which is precisely the Dharma. The preface states: "Attaining this Dharma-gate is truly a marvelous practice. This corresponds to [the following].
This is somewhat similar to those who witness spiritual efficacy, just as Maudgalyāyana appeared in person. "Command" (*ming*) refers to the teaching and commandment.
